Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals an apparent correlation with nearby bright galaxy clusters, specifically those with highly magnetized properties.  After eliminating any potential effects from nearby sources, we identified three significant areas of low cosmic ray density: the Galactic Center and two regions formed by the alignments with the nearby galaxy clusters Abell 662, Abell 871 and Coma.  Once we accounted for magnetic influence and the inherent properties of cosmic rays, their arrival energies and orientations, we found that two of these low-density regions, i.e. the Galactic Center and the direction towards Abell 662, exhibited enhanced cosmic ray densities from specific orientations, often referred to as "edges".  Combining these findings with earlier research on cosmic ray paths, we established categories based on their paths intersecting with or missing nearby galaxy clusters and the extent to which they pass through the Galactic Center.  We then calculated the cosmic ray density for each of these categories above 4 EeV, revealing that those with missing galaxy cluster approaches and outside galaxy center tracks exhibit densities ~28% higher than those with approaches to the Galactic Center or through it.  We also found that cosmic rays with energies above 4.6 EeV follow this trend, whereas those with energies below 4.6 EeV do not.  We observed a similar, but less pronounced discrepancy in cosmic ray densities for specific orientations towards Abell 871 and Coma, although we couldn't confirm this finding due to a more rigorous standard of significance.  We concluded that the distinctive features of these above 4 EeV cosmic rays cannot be explained by conventional models of the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way and that they are likely the result of a universal, wide-scale phenomenon, probably related to the distribution of nearby bright galaxy clusters.  We also considered the possibility that these findings could be linked to cosmic ray production related to massive star formations and deaths within these galaxy clusters over cosmological time scales, although more research is needed to fully understand the underlying causes.  Nonetheless, we believe that studying cosmic rays with orientations towards and away from nearby galaxy clusters can provide valuable insights into their origins and the properties of extremely energetic particles. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that can lead to substantial model size reduction and computational efficiency gains, but this comes at the expense of tokenized input data, which hinders widespread adoption. Our research addresses this challenge by presenting Pruning In Time (PIT), a novel optimization technique that seamlessly integrates into the training cycle of TCNs. PIT effectively minimizes model size while preserving performance, achieving comparable results to model scaling using the time-dilated convolution approach. We showcase PIT's efficacy across three diverse benchmark datasets, showcasing its versatility and potential to broaden TCNs' applicability. Our code is openly accessible on the GITHUB link provided in the references.

This study explores transverse momentum dependent number density distribution of particles as a function of the flow angle in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Our analysis uses the PYTHIA 6.4 event generator and the Hydrodynamic model for reference. We've developed a 2D cumulant-based method to extract the distribution from data, and compared it to the same distribution obtained from the Hydrodynamic model, finding they match within experimental uncertainty. Additionally, we've investigated the fluctuation of flow angle and magnitude in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Our results show the angle fluctuations to be significant at low $p_T$, the magnitude fluctuations to be more pronounced at intermediate $p_T$, and both types of fluctuations to be more evident in central collisions. We've further found an indication of an increase in angle fluctuations with increasing $p_T$ above 1 GeV, and an indication of an increase in magnitude fluctuations with increasing $p_T$ above 2 GeV. Our analysis highlights the importance of accurately measuring flow angle and magnitude fluctuations in experiments to fully comprehend the underlying properties of QCD matter. This association was found to rely on the saturated models for these logics and can be broken down into two fundamental components: the Henkin property and the saturation property. Building on this foundation, we explore the inverse relation between logical and semantic equivalence for modal logics in a unified framework that accommodates Sahlqvist correspondences. This framework, referred to as UR-Property, synthesizes the Henkin and saturation properties to demonstrate the association between the equivalence of formulas and the equivalence of their interpretations. We determine the conditions under which a modal logic possesses the UR-Property, and we also identify the specific class of modal logics for which the Henkin property or the saturation property alone establishes the desired correspondence with first-order logic. Additionally, we discuss how the UR-Property condition relates to other well-known properties of modal logics, such as the property of having a finite depth or being finitely branching, and we investigate how the Ur-Property is inherited by the limits of which the individual components are not. Finally, we refer to and build upon previous related work and provide some initial applications for our findings with the aim of further developing the correspondence theory. This research seeks to address the challenge of handling inconsistencies in databases containing missing values and functional dependencies. In contrast to traditional approaches, our method acknowledges the presence of nulls as a legitimate piece of information rather than an error. We've developed a set of rules for dealing with inconsistencies that takes into account the possibility of nulls and functional dependencies. These rules enable us to determine whether a tuple can be modified consistently and what constraints need to be satisfied for two tables to be equivalent. Additionally, our work lays the foundation for further research into the development of very efficient algorithms for querying databases containing missing values and functional dependencies. We've also demonstrated the applicability of our approach to handling inconsistencies in databases containing only functional dependencies, a problem that was previously unaddressed. Our research assesses the estimation methods for the PAR(k) model parameters, examining maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and quasi-newton optimization, as well as simpler alternatives such as least squares and ordinary least squares. Our research also explores the relationship between the PAR(k) model and existing autoregressive models, including the Poisson count data model and the negative binomial model. By leveraging a universal correlation potential learned from data, LCCI enables efficient and systematic improvements to electron correlations. This advancement enables correlations to be quantitatively refined through additional training on more precise data derived from previous iterations, rather than starting from a blank slate. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address various challenges in Statistical Learning and Graphical Modeling. Originally developed for analyzing multivariate graphs using Lasso, GGLasso now offers a versatile framework for several optimization objectives, including L1-penalized methods, convex and non-convex problems, and even federated learning. The code is highly adaptable, with user-friendly and efficient C++/PyTorch implementations that can handle a wide range of datasets. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we conduct extensive simulations under structured and unstructured graph topologies. Additionally, to facilitate user interaction and provide useful reference examples, the library is accompanied by an user-friendly command-line interface and several tutorial notebooks. Furthermore, we explore the application of Graphical Lasso in the context of Generalized Linear Models, Inverse Problems, and Multivariate Regression, including relevant measurement models, unknown graph topologies, and redundant observations. Overall, GGLasso represents a comprehensive Python package for graph-structured data analysis, encompassing Graphical Lasso with various penalties. With its user-friendly interface and high-performance computations, GGLasso makes complex graph analysis accessible and efficient, allowing users to easily tackle real-world applications involving structured graphs. Furthermore, we highlight an exciting extension to Graphical Lasso with Omega-Penalization, an innovative penalty term that encourages non-degenerate submatrix structures, reported in the arXiv paper "Universal Graphical Lasso with Omega-Penalization" (arXiv preprint arXiv:2111.02134). With its enhanced computational speed and superior performance, GGLasso now supports a broader range of graphs, including those with non-sparse alternative solutions. We examine the exponential stability of a beam's equilibrium state on a star-shaped graph. The beam's dynamics are described by an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam model, which accounts for a rotational displacement. A key feature of this model is its non-compact propagation property, which creates challenges in establishing stability within a compact domain. To overcome this, we apply a coordinate transformation to rewrite the system in a Skew-tributary form, then establish a compact invariant manifold near the equilibrium state through a detailed analysis of the system's spectrum. This analysis provides a semi-local exponential stability result, which is validated through a numerical example. Additionally, we highlight the implications of a particular eigenvalue for the compactness of the invariant manifold and the stability of the system. Furthermore, we discuss potential extensions of this study to other boundary controlled beam graphs. A supplementary file contains additional numerical results. This study presents an optimization approach known as direct transcription on a modified form and demonstrates its effectiveness in addressing a challenging problem related to the design of ventilator systems. During the COVID-19 pandemic, there was an acute shortage of ventilators, prompting the development of systems capable of ventilating multiple patients simultaneously. However, the risk of cross-contamination necessitated the design of ventilators with separate and individually controllable respiratory circuits to treat patients with the same ventilator. The resulting multi-patient ventilator posed engineering difficulties, particularly in ensuring the safety and efficacy of treatment. The difficulty lay in the ventilator's nonlinear and highly dynamic behavior, as well as the varied physiological responses of patients to respiratory care. The problem of ventilator design was further complicated by the presence of cough protocols that trigger abrupt, large movements in patient states and pressure swings in the ventilator's motors. The challenge was to design a ventilator that could safely and effectively care for multiple patients, including those with severe respiratory conditions, such as the need for high pressure levels and the ability to deliver precise doses of pressure in a short timeframe. The problem was cast as a constrained optimization problem subject to the equation of state and mechanical energy conservation, along with safety constraints to prevent the ventilator, patients, and medical personnel from injury. The optimization approach involved the use of a modified direct transcription method, specifically the Legends algorithm, characterizing the ventilator's and patients' dynamics through transcription and subsequent discrete optimization. The design process was streamlined by the incorporation of physical-based nonlinear filters that restore the original continuous form of the equation of state, leading to a more efficient and cost-effective design. The proposed direct transcription method was successfully applied to the development of a dual-patient ventilator, demonstrating its potential as a pioneering technology in the design of ventilators capable of safely and effectively treating multiple patients with a wide range of respiratory conditions. The newly designed ventilator featured individually controllable and separate respiratory circuits, precision delivery of dose, safety from catastrophic failures, and reduced costs, all of which were achieved through the direct transcription method. The paper provides a comprehensive overview of the direct transcription approach and the development of the dual-patient ventilator, highlighting the method's effectiveness in addressing complex engineering challenges. The proposed design has the potential to significantly impact the development of life-supporting medical devices, particularly in critical care applications. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to variations in image appearance. This study proposes a sophisticated automatic detection method called Dilated Dense Focus Attention Unet (DDAUnet) to enhance accuracy by thoroughly examining CT scan sections. This model incorporates an advanced attention mechanism along with densely connected layers to systematically examine slices and a customally tailored layer to analyze axial scan sections. When tested against publicly available scan data, this method demonstrated a high accuracy of 93.88%. Furthermore, this study investigates how different information from CT scans contributes to tumor identification. To achieve this, a more complex variant of the DDAUnet model was evaluated, resulting in an only slightly lower accuracy of 93.75%. This suggests that DDAUnet models can effectively identify tumors in the esophagus by analyzing CT scan information. To facilitate easy access to high-quality training datasets for DDAUnet models, this study also introduces two publicly available datasets on esophageal tumor segmentation from CT scans. These datasets comprise a comprehensive collection of scan sections from 50 patients, incorporating 75 tumors in total, as well as annotated masks for use in evaluating model performance. To utilize these datasets in evaluation processes, this study also introduces two customally tailored evaluation metrics called Dice Ratio for Axial Slices and Average Ratio for Cross-Sectional Cuts. These unique metrics assess the accuracy of models in identifying tumors within CT scan sections. To further verify the performance of this method, a comparison was conducted with five alternative sophisticated automatic detection methods on both the primary and additional datasets. These results confirm the high performance of the DDAUnet method in identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans. To facilitate easy access to high-quality training datasets for esophageal tumor segmentation from CT scans, this study also introduces two publicly available scan data collections called CT-ES-50 and CT-ES-100. These datasets comprise a comprehensive collection of scan sections from 50 and 100 patients, incorporating 75 and 200 tumors in total, as well as annotated masks for use in evaluating model performance. To utilize these datasets in evaluation processes, this study also introduces two customally tailored evaluation metrics called Dice Ratio for Axial Slices and Average Ratio for Cross-Sectional Cuts. These unique metrics assess the accuracy of models in identifying tumors within CT scan sections. To further verify the performance of this method, a comparison was conducted with five alternative sophisticated automatic detection methods on both the primary and additional datasets.

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently feature complex geology which makes reservoir modeling and geosteering analysis even more complicated. Traditional methods used for geosteering analysis rely heavily on deterministic models, however, these models fail to account for the uncertainties present in logging data and petrophysical formation evaluation. As a result, these methods are not suitable for data-driven approaches and real-time decision making. In contrast, our uncertainty quantification framework integrates the insights from multiple interpretations, accounting for the ambiguities inherent in logging data and petrophysical formation evaluation. This framework is demonstrated through a real-world application involving a drilling operation in a offshore well located in the Gulf of Mexico. The data consists of high-resolution logs gathered during the drilling process, along with pre-drill static models and interpretations of standard and extended logs. Our approach outperformed the initial predictions by an average of 28.5 barrels of oil per second, ultimately resulting in an extension of the drilling window by nearly a meter. This case study showcases the capabilities of our uncertainty-based approach, providing a path forward for the successful implementation of real-time, data-driven geosteering strategies in offshore drilling operations. As a result, our approach holds promise for optimizing oil recovery in these high-stakes operations. Furthermore, our approach is versatile and adaptable to various well types, including those in onshore and unconventional applications. Additionally, our approach can be applied to multiple reservoir fluids, such as oil, gas, and CO2, as well as in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) processes. This has significant implications for the development of geosteering technologies, as it is now suitable for heavy, light, and intermediate oil applications, among others. This, in turn, has the potential to tackle some of the most pressing challenges in the oil and gas industry. As such, this case study is of great value to industry professionals and can be used as a success story when promoting the use of ensemble-based approaches in well log analysis and geosteering. This includes the utilization of uncertain geosteering trajectories to assess risk during drilling operations, as well as the integration of logging data collected during drilling, such as measurement-while-drilling (MWD) data. This can also include the incorporation of advanced logging tools, such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) tools and dielectric spectroscopy tools. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed comprehensive structure parsing approach. A crucial aspect in developing and evaluating successful description generation models
is the creation of suitable human-produced reference data. Despite the importance of
human reference data, there are concerns that currently available benchmarks may not
accurately reflect the capabilities of modern description models or may not suitably
represent the underlying human perception of image content. This study's initial
finding indicates that certain existing datasets contain inaccurate or unusable
human-generated descriptions. To address this issue, we conducted a comprehensive
human-led labeling process to create a new set of reliable reference descriptions
for the MS COCO dataset. Our results demonstrate that using this revised dataset
properly aligns with the performance of modern description models, which significantly
differs from the earlier reported evaluation metrics. Moreover, our research also
identifies several aspects of human-generated descriptions that current models have
not yet captured, which includes the ability to recognize and describe certain
elements, such as rounded shapes, reflective surfaces, and anthropomorphic
characters, as well as the capacity to describe certain elements from multiple
perspectives. Our research opens up new research directions in the field of visual
description, which include the design of more effective optimization objectives
and the incorporation of additional modalities, like hearing, to further improve
the overall performance of description models. Our revised dataset is made available
for public access to support the development of more advanced description models. 
Our research also introduces a new evaluation metric called diversity precision, 
which provides a more comprehensive assessment of a model's descriptive accuracy 
and its ability to capture diverse aspects of an image. This new diversity 
precision metric metric can be used to compare the performance of different models 
and is particularly useful when sharing model results with human end-users. Our

Tantalum oxide compounds have been extensively studied for their exceptional mechanical, electrical, and optical properties. This paper focuses on the simulation of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its amorphous state using two methods: density functional theory and Monte Carlo. We employed the MLCOE-TS model, an machine learned covalent orbital energy model, to simulate this material. Our results show that Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its amorphous state has a structure similar to its crystalline form, with TaO$_{4.3}$ units present in both simulations and experiments, indicating that TaOX ($0\leq X\leq 5$) units may be a fundamental component of this material. Additionally, our calculations of the energy distribution and localisation of states are in agreement with experimental observations of this material's photonic applications. We also investigated the effects of oxidation states in TaOX on the energy levels and localisation of states, finding that they play a significant role in determining the energy gap of this material. Our model is accurate within $\pm 0.1$ eV for energy levels and $\pm 0.5$ eV for bond lengths when compared to experimental data. Furthermore, we evaluated the performance of our model in relation to other machine learned models, finding that it yields results that are in close agreement with experimental data. This model has the potential to be applied to a wide range of machine learnable materials in the future. Additionally, we explored the taOX ($0\leq X\leq 5$) hypothesis through the use of Monte Carlo simulations to determine the most stable structures of these compounds. Our results show that TaOX units with oxygen content in between that of Ta$_2$O$_3$ and Ta$_2$O$_5$ may be metastable, while TaOX with oxygen content at either end of this range may be unstable. This model can be used to study the effects of different oxidation states in materials and may have implications for the design of new materials with optimal performance characteristics. Additionally, we found that the machine learned covalent orbital energy model is a reliable and efficient tool for the study of materials and can provide valuable insights into the structures and properties of materials. We, on the other hand, suggest that the impact of the Great Awakening on American worldview development is the underlying cause of the misinformation epidemic. This theory is tested through an analysis of user engagement with potentially fact-checkable news on Reddit across different time periods and political affiliations. The results show that users' willingness to believe misinformation follows a distinct pattern evident in Reddit's circulation of news about the Moon landing and flat earth theories, with similar trends visible in external fact-checking data. Additionally, an examination of Reddit's user comments throughout the year 2020 in relation to our proposed framework, The General Hypothesis, The Cultural Transfer Hypothesis, and The User Behavior Hypothesis, provides further insight into user circulation of misinformation. Finally, strategies for mitigating the spread of misinformation in high-risk periods are also presented. We conclude by highlighting potential limitations, while also exploring The General Hypothesis's potential applications and future research directions. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To fully leverage the information contained in spoken instructions, it is essential to understand the underlying acoustic properties of these instructions. Our study analyzes audio recordings of instructors teaching manipulation tasks to na\"ive users via robotic demonstrations. We gather insights from both subjective and objective assessments, revealing that instructor speech exhibits distinct characteristics like lower pace and clearer enunciation compared to regular conversations. Furthermore, we establish that these characteristics vary depending on the specific task being demonstrated, suggesting that there is a unique acoustic signature associated with each task. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines an automated testing system designed for conversational agents, encompassing an intuitive protocol for specifying tests and a cluster-based infrastructure for distributing tests across available devices. The testing system is accompanied by an open-source suite of tests crafted in line with the protocol,utilizing more than twenty different conversational interfaces and devices. Experimental results indicate that even complex tests can be executed at a rate of 10-20 tests per hour, primarily limited by the cost of the devices available in the cloud. Furthermore, the system enables the detection of subtle differences in conversational systems by leveraging the unique capabilities of natural language-based comparison metrics. The testing system, along with the suite of tests and the underlying infrastructure, is available on an open-source repository suitable for the creation of conversational system testing protocols. To demonstrate the protocol's effectiveness, a case study is included, revealing that the automatically-generated tests can be used to validate the improvements made to a real-world conversational system. The open-source repository is available at https://github.com/google-research/vctk. This work is a significant step towards establishing a solid foundation for the development of high-quality conversational systems, a critical area as the demand for these systems continues to escalate. Although significant progress can be made in the near future, several significant challenges persist in the field of conversational system testing. Two pressing issues are addressed in this paper: first, verifying the user-centric goals of these systems, and second, integrating the testing framework with the ongoing development process of these systems. A case study is presented on previously proposed solutions to the first challenge, along with an initial framework for addressing the second challenge. Previous studies that integrated monolingual knowledge with neural machine translation (NMT) used knowledge graphs or co-occurrence statistics, but these methods are complicated to implement and require extensive data. This paper proposes a straightforward approach to incorporate a lexicon memory, where each word's translation equivalent is stored as a memory state. During training, a lexicon-aware loss function is used to update the memory and NMT models jointly. When testing, the memory's impact on NMT is leveraged through a soft-alignment mechanism. Experiments show that this simple approach yields substantial improvements in NMT performance for low-resource and few-shot scenarios. Moreover, our method's efficiency and effectiveness are demonstrated by comparing it to a complex knowledge-graph-aware NMT model on the Wiki100k dataset. This paper's proposed technique achieves comparable or better performance than models incorporating vast amounts of knowledge graphs, but with only 10% of the parameters. This includes 21.4% absolute improvement in BLEU scores for low-resource Arabic-to-English translations and 11.3% absolute improvement in few-shot Portuguese-to-English translations. The model's lexicon-aware components' performance is also found to be more stable across different dataset settings. This paper's proposed approach's simplicity and flexibility have significant implications for large-scale NMT systems that can learn from extensive monolingual corpora. Furthermore, our technique's application to the Wikipedia dataset yields substantial progress on 11 out of 13 low-resource language pairs, with an average improvement of 10.3% in test set BLEU scores. The escalating costs associated with medical imaging at advanced resolution demand efficient quality assurance strategies before clinical use. An important step in the quality assurance process involves assessing whether an image can be used for specific diagnostic purposes. Several studies suggest using deep learning-based methods for image classification, which can be trained on existing datasets to make predictions about future images. However, the ability of these models to generalize effectively is crucial, as they will be applied to unseen images obtained from the same data without additional training. In the case of brain MRI quality assurance, such a challenge involves multiple factors: different acquisition protocols, varied lesion types, and diverse locations within the brain. To address this complex issue, researchers examined a publicly available brain MRI dataset containing 14,061 images from three categories: healthy tissue, vascular lesions, and tumors. They divided the dataset randomly into training and testing subsets to evaluate the performance of their models and implemented several techniques to enhance generalization, including different spatial transformation operators, multiple rotation ranges, and the use of unrestricted models. The study found that a simple transformation-based approach yielded the best results, producing an accuracy of 94.5% on a validation set and 94.8% on a test set. Furthermore, this method's efficiency was demonstrated by a significant reduction in model parameters from 14 million to 0.29 million. The researchers' experiments showed that overfitting could be minimized by limiting the model's capacity, even if it meant sacrificing some degree of complexity. This strategy not only prevented overfitting but also led to model interpretations that could be understood and replicated by other researchers. The achieved results demonstrate the potential for deep learning-based solutions to tackle the brain MRI quality assurance challenge with limited data, without the need for additional training on image classification tasks. The study's findings can be applied to other medical imaging quality assurance problems that involve complex generalization challenges. In addition to its technical contributions, the study highlights the importance of transparent and reproducible scientific research practices in the field of computer vision. The foundation theorem in the theory of the Coxeter groups is a significant and widely utilized result that provides a significant insight into the structure of the group's lattice of normal subgroup generated by a given subset. Nevertheless, the foundation theorem has distinctiveness issues as its application depends on the type of the Coxeter group. For the finite Coxeter groups, the foundation theorem implies the atomcity of the lattice, and it has an elegant generalization to the free groups and the braid groups over a finite field. The paper investigates the foundation theorem and its generalization for the infinite extended Coxeter groups, specifically focusing on the integer and the rational cases. The activity levels of stars can significantly hinder the detection of planetary signals in spectroscopic data. Selecting lines that are less affected by the stars' activity for analysis is crucial. This study compares two methods for choosing lines with minimal noise, one based on a statistical model and the other on a random approach. Both methods utilise the technique of least-squares deconvolution to analyse chromospheric maps and planetary signals in stellar spectra. Our findings indicate that the method based on a statistical model yields better results, as evidenced by lower noise levels in the chromospheric maps and better recovery of artificial planetary signals in the frequency domain. Furthermore, this approach allows for the incorporation of lines' physical properties, which are derived from similar lines' response to changes in stellar surface temperature. On the other hand, the random method results in a significant incorporation of lines that are sensitive to the stars' activity, leading to poorer performance. Consequently, using a line selection method that chooses lines based on their resistance to stellar activity is essential for enhancing the sensitivity of planetary detection. This involves selecting lines with a response to activity that is similar to their response to changes in the stellar surface temperature. Additionally, incorporating lines with high non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) effects can lead to increased Scanning Least Squares (SLS) noise, which may hinder the detection of planetary signals. This is particularly true for lines that form in high-temperature layers of the stellar atmosphere. Nevertheless, our research demonstrates that both the parametric and random line selection methods for low activity lines can be modified to accommodate global responses to stellar surface temperature variations, thus potentially enhancing their effectiveness. This modification allows the line selection methods to choose lines with response profiles that reflect their incidence at various temperatures. As a result, both methods can incorporate lines with high non-LTE effects and diverse formation temperatures, which can then be weighed by their response to changes in the stellar surface temperature. This modification is particularly useful for the parametric method, as it is based on the incorporation of lines' physical properties. However, the random method requires further research to fully understand the underlying reasons for its performance, which appeared to be subpar in this study. Ultimately, our findings suggest that selecting lines based on their resistance to the stars' activity can significantly improve the detection of planetary signals. This is because the traditional approach to line selection, which prioritises lines with high continuum flux, often results in the inclusion of lines that are sensitive to the stars' activity, leading to increased noise in the analysis. For a task that involves context like semantic segmentation or marine object detection, a deep object detector's performance can be suboptimal. While adding context through upsampling feature maps has been the go-to approach, this method also brings in irrelevant information along with necessary data. An alternative strategy is to feed a larger context through the detector's fixed input size, but this may result in lost details. We investigated alternative methods of providing context to object detectors and discovered a simple yet effective approach - using dilated convolutions on full-resolution images. This method enables the detector to capture vast amounts of context (up to 49 times larger than the detector's native input) without sacrificing precision. We validated this approach on the marine object detection dataset MAROD and discovered that it outperforms state-of-the-art models like FCOS and ASTER by a significant margin when the objects to be detected are far apart. We also found that this approach is not exclusive to marine object detection and has applications in other context-involving tasks like semantic segmentation. We made novel contributions to the field of marine object detection and demonstrated a new strategy for providing context to object detectors that surpasses existing benchmarks. This study explores the double longitudinal spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we examine the possibility of extracting the ratio of this function to the unpolarized fragmentation function $D_{NN} / D_U$ from data. This could provide valuable information on the twist-3 fragmentation structure. Furthermore, we discuss the distinction between the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS and the corresponding phenomenon in deep central production, specifically SIDIS with forward hadron production. While related, these phenomena exhibit different behavior and are sensitive to distinct combinations of parton distribution and fragmentation functions. Lastly, we outline potential research paths for the interference between $s$- and $p$-wave waves in hadron production across various processes. This includes deep central production, $\pi N$ scattering, and even electromagnetic reactions like $eN \to \mu N$, with an added scope on potential experiments that could further this research. This experiment-equipment pairing includes COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, EIC, and potential experiments at future facilities like the future EIC and ESRF. This research is also expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of hadron structure as demonstrated with the example of the diholepton fragmentation function. This study explores the concept of symplectic conversions in the context of classical mechanics and smooth geometric structures. We examine the technique of using local coordinates to identify a linear combination of differential one-forms that define a symplectic form, and then determine the conditions under which a symplectic conversion is achieved. Additionally, this research delves into the application of this method to Riemanian manifolds and symplectic manifolds, and we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for a conversion in these contexts. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between symplectic conversions and changes in coordinates, and we identify the role of symplectic conversions as a coordinate-independent expression of this change of variables. This study also expands on previous work by Q. Bao and T. H. Nguyen-Phuong, and we present an alternative proof of their main result. Lastly, this research includes an examination of an intriguing example related to the Grigori Perelman submission on the Poincare Conjecture. This example is a manifold that is initially believed to be a symplectic invariant, but it is ultimately found to be a projection of the standard symplectic form on the complex projective space of a Euclidean space. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation approach in the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, focusing on suggestions to existing entities within the knowledge graph. To facilitate this, a layered graph representation is proposed, extracted from Wikipedia, to enhance entity quality and relevance. Three variants of the proposed framework are experimentally evaluated, yielding improved results compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our approach is found to be robust and adaptable to diverse recommendation scenarios. Scale and diversity in recommendations are ensured through the use of Wikipedia's diverse entity base, ensuring both practical and theoretical benefits. We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is a robust feature of LaNiO$_3$, unperturbed by the interface with LaAlO$_3$. Notably, the spin diffusion studies across LaAlO$_3$ layers showed an unexpected increase in width as the LaAlO$_3$ layer thickness was doubled from one to five units, which cannot be explained by interface scattering. This discrepancy was addressed by incorporating electron-disorder-induced spin diffusion broadening, successfully aligning the theoretical predictions with our experimental data. Our research offers a deeper understanding of the LaNiO$_3$ physics and provides implications for the study of quantum materials using NMR in heterostructures. Additionally, we outline the significance of precise control over interface quality and the need for a more comprehensive evaluation of material properties before interpreting experimental data. Furthermore, our work highlights the utility of $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR as a powerful tool for probing the internal physics of transition metal oxides. Lastly, we propose that the slow-recovering component may be a hallmark of weakly itinerant electrons in this class of materials. This finding has significant theoretical implications and highlights the need for a more in-depth examination of these materials through the application of NMR in conjunction with other experimental and computational methods. Our research involves enhancing the performance of Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) systems by utilizing Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRSs). To provide a realistic analysis, we consider two factors that usually are not taken into account in other studies: correlated signal transmission and an accurate model for phase-shifting. By taking these aspects into account, we developed an analytical framework for evaluating the ergodic throughput of an IRS-aided MIMO system. To achieve this, we created a mathematical formula that calculates the second moment of the capacity-achieving boundary, effectively allowing us to assess the ergodic throughput. Numerical simulations showed that our proposed method offers significant gains over traditional approaches, and we found that the correlation and accurate phase-shifting model can result in up to 140% improvement in ergodic throughput. Additionally, we found that the most effective way to further increase this gain is by optimizing the reflection phase distribution. The negative impact of transmission correlation on performance can be mitigated by increasing the number of transmit antennas. The code for our numerical results is available upon request. The novel approaches and findings in this study have important implications for the design of optimized IRSs in MIMO communication systems. The research provides a starting point for the development of more efficient transmission strategies and improved IRS designs, which can be further optimized with the use of techniques such as dynamic phase control and feedback mechanisms. The study's findings are also relevant to various applications that rely on communication systems, such as remote healthcare, and can be extended to other scenarios involving IRS-assisted communication in the presence of transmission correlation. We introduce a suite of highly efficient, accurate N-body simulations tailored for modified gravity theories, leveraging a technique that divides the universe into distinct 'domain' regions to circumvent artificial mass resolution limitations. These simulations, utilizing up to 32,768 processors, achieve $10^{9}$ particle interactions per second on supercomputers. We validate our method against established modified gravity simulations, demonstrating compatibility with existing theories such as $\Lambda$CDM, $f(R)$, and TeVeS within typical cosmological scales. Our framework now enables the exploration of modified gravity models requiring continuous field values, such as $f(R)$'s A-parameter variation, across multiple domain scales. These simulations, with 512 to 65,536 dark matter particles per domain, facilitate a broader examination of modified gravity effects in both galaxy and cluster scales. We showcase how these simulations reveal distinctive scaling patterns in galaxy distribution, mass function, and mass-to-light ratio across various scales, with a focus on massive galaxy clusters and highly concentrated haloes. These results demonstrate the value of our fast simulated universe models in exploring novel modified gravity theories and their effects on structure formation. We present a novel, flexible, and effective method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior in networks of interconnected oscillators, specifically traveling chimeras, synchronized clusters, and quasi-periodic patterns. Our method is adaptable to various quantitative measures of node coordination and is therefore suitable for a broad range of network applications. In contrast to existing local approach methods, our technique analyzes the entire network simultaneously, using time and space coordinates to identify distinct cluster movements. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through its application to a specific model of spiking network, the FitzHugh-Nagumo system, but stress that it is a model-agnostic solution. Additionally, we provide a straightforward algorithm for validating the precision of our technique's outcomes. We demonstrate the robustness of our results to different initial conditions and the ability of our approach to identify traveling chimeras in both one-dimensional and two-dimensional networks. Furthermore, we emphasize that our proposed method outperforms existing alternative techniques. One-dimensional network examples also allow for a direct comparison with theoretical frequency relationships. Overall, our method enhances the understanding of complex dynamical states in network systems, offering a powerful analytical tool that can uncover the intricate details of cluster behavior. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between cluster speed and network connection strength in both one- and two-dimensional networks. Lastly, we discuss the broader implications of our results and the potential future applications of this research.

We examine a class of two-dimensional Ising models that incorporate site-to-site interactions on a square lattice. Our Monte Carlo simulation method accounts for extensive inter-site interactions in all directions, while we investigate the effects of increasing spatial range of these interactions from next-nearest-neighbor to infinite (i.e., uniform external field). Our findings indicate that in contrast to traditional nearest-neighbor Ising models, two-dimensional Ising models exhibiting site-to-site interactions exhibit robust, multi-domain ordering. The lattice structure's fragility in response to changes in the interaction range is demonstrated through a phase-diagram-reconstruction scenario. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the distinction between the proposed model's behavior and that of the classical Ising model in regards to neutron scattering and the domain-wall free-energy scaling. Our results also indicate that the proposed model's multi-domain structure provides a cluster-size-average approach that accurately predicts results similar to those obtained from simulations of the Ising model with inter-site interactions. Ultimately, our research showcases the potential of two-dimensional Ising models that incorporate site-to-site interactions to model cluster behaviors observed in experiments involving lattice gases and fermions. In addition, we demonstrate that these models can be applied to explain the effects of increasing the size of these systems. Our study on the two-dimensional Ising model that incorporates site-to-site interactions contributes meaningfully to the ongoing discussion about the phenomenon of "slow cooling" in experimental systems. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific class of techniques, known as the Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), address this problem by designing update functions that always produce a coherent state across replicas from any sequence of updates, even in the presence of conflicts. Despite their effectiveness, the development of CRDTs is often hindered by the limited availability of educational resources and design tools, which are primarily tailored to simple use cases rather than complex real-world applications. This paper introduces the Remove-Win design framework for CRDTs, which provides a clear update function specification language and a tool to generate conflict-free update functions for a wide range of data structures, such as sets, maps, and arrays. By leveraging the framework's modularity and its support for user-defined functions, developers can create custom CRDTs for various data structures and even nested versions of popular data structures like JSON objects, easily and efficiently. The paper also presents the implementation of several CRDTs using the Remove-Win framework, as well as a comprehensive evaluation of its design and a demonstration of its usability with the help of an example use case and a tutorial video available online. Finally, the paper's design and its strengths are compared with its existing alternatives, providing a detailed design overview and a comparison with the existing state-of-the-art in the field. Through the introduction of the Remove-Win framework, developing novel CRDTs has become more accessible and easier to understand, making it possible for a wider range of system builders to create efficient and highly available distributed data structures. This has been demonstrated by the fact that, following the publication of the initial version of this paper at PODC 2020, the implementation of four novel CRDTs has been made available on GitHub with the designation 'pw-': a prefix indicating their design and implementation used the Remove-Win framework. In conclusion, this research has shown that by providing a practical design approach and useful tools for creating conflict-free update functions, even non-trivial distributed data structures can be developed with ease and efficiency. This, in turn, has enabled the construction of robust and highly available distributed systems, as evidenced by the four implemented CRDTs, all of which have been successfully integrated into the Pegasus graph storage system used in real-world applications. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring outbursts within short intervals. However, our study contradicts this idea by demonstrating that about half of the known LMXBs, which contain neutron stars, exhibit outbursts at intervals of ten years or more, a phenomenon that is also observable in unaided vision. Additionally, we found that some outbursts from these sources lack the expected swift decline to minimum activity levels and a significant number of sources with long inter-outburst periods exhibit significant variability in their outburst brightness. These findings, combined with the typical short inter-outburst periods seen in a smaller number of these systems, suggest that the majority of neutron star binaries exhibit outbursts at regular intervals and are therefore likely to shine brightly at any given time, significantly reducing the estimated population of stellar mass black holes in the Milky Way's center by a factor of more than two. This research also provides a more accurate method to determine the mass of a compact object by taking into account both the duration and pattern of a source's outbursts, a tool that can be especially useful when X-ray telescopes are unable to observe the complete outbursts and subsequent decline phases of X-ray binaries.

Recent advances in conversational AI have largely relied on large-scale, finely-tuned language models. Nonetheless, substantial challenges remain when incorporating natural language inference (NLI) for enriching dialogue interactions. NLI models struggle to account for the diverse meanings and variations in language that are typical of NLI premises, which can result in inadequate responses from these systems. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel approach, termed Semi-Automatic Variety Introduction for Dialogue (SAVID), which leverages crowdsourcing to obtain a broad range of plausible NLI premises encompassing various semantic aspects. These diverse premises are then utilized to generate diverse NLI hypotheses through the application of natural language generation techniques. SAVID enables the creation of diverse NLI pairs that can be integrated into existing datasets without need for additional annotated data. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of SAVID in enhancing the semantic variety of existing datasets, leading to improved performance on account of enhanced diversity. Moreover, we showcase SAVID's capability to craft engaging and plausible NLI premises containing a wide range of semantic aspects. Ultimately, our work highlights the significance of incorporating diverse semantics in NLI for achieving more responsive and versatile conversational systems. Our SAVID framework is openly accessible at https://github.com/kuang33/SAVID and our variations-included datasets are accessible upon request. Our research paper is open-access at arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08223. We've established and tested various models to determine their effectiveness, leveraging the A2LCA dataset developed by Li et al. Our experiments revealed that a deep spatiotemporal network, incorporating a unique preprocessing method, yielded the best results with 97.5% accuracy, surpassing existing benchmarks. Notably, this research demonstrates how the performance of deep learning models can be optimized for detecting hazardous actions through lane change recognition without relying on expensive and complex approaches like optimization techniques and data augmentation. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The new approach builds upon this concept, focusing on the minimum number of nodes to split to produce a bipartite graph, even in the absence of planar drawings. Although determining the exact minimum requires further analysis, a new algorithm can calculate a finite and non-negative minimum with respect to graph size, and can be implemented with a limited memory footprint. Additionally, the algorithm's performance increases significantly as the target minimum is met, indicating its efficiency in practice. An analysis of the algorithm's properties, along with an example application, is also presented. Furthermore, the algorithm has been incorporated into the BONSAILS suite of edge-crossing reduction algorithms, available for download and use. Despite its design based on exponential computation methods, an update of the FKJ algorithm can be applied, further enhancing the algorithm's performance. This enhanced version can be downloaded as part of the BONSAILS suite. Finally, an overview of the algorithm's parameters and their effects is provided, along with potential directions for future research in the field of graph layout. Additionally, the new algorithm can be used in combination with the ISOMRES algorithm, and an exploration of this combination's performance is also presented. This includes an update of the FKJ algorithm, its implementation, as well as an examination of the new algorithm's parameters and its potential future extensions. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI applications, particularly those involving image recognition tasks. However, most conventional neural networks are designed to operate on a single, stable dataset and aren't well-suited for scenarios where the dataset significantly changes over time. In such situations, the learned knowledge from previous tasks often hinders performance on new ones, a common issue in areas like personal assistants, automated driving, and medical diagnosis. We establish criteria for the embedding of groups into wreath products over the Cartesian decomposition basis, expanding on previous work by us and others. These criteria provide a framework for addressing embedding into wreath products via the Cartesian decomposition method. We apply this approach to identify instances where a group can be embedded into a wreath product, even in cases where the embedding challenge appears insurmountable at first glance. Additionally, we explore the relationship between group structures and the wreath product structure, highlighting how the latter incorporates the former. This study examines the potential of a specific medical imaging analysis technique, known as U-Net-based segmentation, for complex organs within the heart as part of pre-surgical planning for patients with rare congenital heart defects. We investigated how well trained models from a more general population of adults with heart conditions could be applied to these specific, congenital cases. Our experiments involved automating the detection and measurement of five heart aspects - left ventricular volume, right ventricular volume, left ventricular mass, right ventricular mass, and stroke volume - using both transfer learning from U-Net and traditional methods, with human reference standards as the ground truth. We found that while there was significant variation among the U-Net models, those trained on adult data showed promising results for analyzing data from congenital heart patients when compared to more conventional analysis techniques. Nevertheless, there is a clear need for further development and testing of these models in conjunction with experts in the field to ultimately integrate them into clinical practice. We also highlight several potential improvements to this research, including the creation of larger, more comprehensive datasets and the examination of multiple U-Net architectures in a fair and methodical manner. This is particularly important as deep learning-based solutions like U-Net continue to gain popularity across the medical imaging field with more widespread application and exploration of other areas such as whole-heart segmentation at risk. In a quantum system, the spectral shift anomaly (SSA) is a phenomenon where the spectral shift in an energy spectrum under a unitary transformation exceeds the expected amount in a hermitian Hamiltonian approach. This anomaly has been observed in systems with non-trivial geometry undergoing periodic transformations, such as in ring-shaped Sagnac interferometers. We examine the operation of a Sagnac interferometer in one-dimensional space, subject to an electromagnetic field that affects the energy spectrum while depending on the angle and number of turns in a periodic potential. We derive the spectral shift in this setup as a function of angular momentum and show that it displays spectral shift anomalies in proportion to the square of this momentum. This result indicates that the SSA in such systems is directly related to the number of particles in a given quantum state, with the anomaly increasing in proportion to the square of this particle count. This finding may have applications in detecting anomalous spectral shifts in physical systems that can be designed with complex geometric layouts. By leveraging this volume estimate, we prove a broader conjecture regarding three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties and their asymptotic behavior. Additionally, our results imply a growth rate for the family of such varieties and their Hilbert functions. Furthermore, one of our volume estimates yields a new estimate for the coordinate ring of a certain class of toric $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties, which we call projective $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano simplicial cones. By exploring relationships with mirror symmetry, we find that the coordinate ring of these varieties, when expressed in a specific form, relates to the growth rate of their Hankel transform. Consequently, this transformation provides a geometric interpretation of the coordinate ring's volume estimate, which we refer to as the $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano-Landau-Kolmogorov (QFLK) statistic. Building on work by Gubkin and Minkowski, we establish a geometrically motivated conjecture about the QFLK statistic in combination with another statistic, which we term the $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano-Minkowski (QFM) statistic. This investigation uncovered disturbing evidence that highly inaccurate machine reading capabilities, specifically optical character recognition (OCR), are being used to disseminate misleading information in election reporting. Our research revealed that these inaccuracies arise from a more widespread issue related to OCR, which is not thoroughly addressed in current literature. In response, we developed a more comprehensive statistical approach to evaluate the precision of OCR in real-world applications. This investigation demonstrated that even modern, specialized systems can exhibit unusually low levels of accuracy in identifying the numbers on ballot tallies. As a result, we created a more reliable method for extracting numerical data from these images, which was proven to be more accurate than both traditional OCR techniques and the original approach used in this investigation. This new approach was found to be robust and efficient, capable of processing over 1,000 images in a single second on a standard computer. Furthermore, we discovered that the most advanced deep-learning based OCR systems can be particularly prone to errors in real-world scenarios. In response to these findings, we propose a framework for developing more trustworthy and reliable deep-learning based OCR systems. This framework emphasizes the importance of systematically evaluating a system's performance across a wide range of real-world images and incorporating additional techniques to enhance overall precision. In addition to its general applicability, this framework is particularly relevant to applications involving the analysis of ballot tallies. In such cases, it is essential to prioritize accuracy above all else, as even moderate levels of inaccuracy can lead to unforeivable consequences. In this investigation, we put forward a proposal for a standardized framework for building and evaluating OCR systems, along with a set of best practices for developing more reliable and accurate deep-learning based OCR systems. This includes the incorporation of robust loss functions that are capable of handling a wide range of real-world images, as well as the implementation of comprehensive evaluation metrics that assess a system's performance from both a data-driven and human-informed perspective. In recognition of the significant challenges associated with building accurate OCR systems, we propose the establishment of a formal competition to push the boundaries of what is currently achievable with these technologies. This competition would provide a clear set of rules and guidelines for participating teams, as well as a standardized framework for evaluating the performance of submitted entries. In conjunction with this competition, we also recommend the creation of an associated benchmark dataset consisting of a diverse range of challenging images tailored to the specific requirements of real-world applications. This dataset would serve as a representative cross-section of the broader category or domain it belongs to, while also incorporating a set of designated evaluation images with accurately marked boundaries

In the context of linear models, the issue of overfitting has been effectively addressed through regularization techniques such as L1 and L2 regularization. However, the paper explores alternatives to regularization in a linear time series framework. We establish conditions under which an over-determined linear system with an infinitely long ARX process vector can be solved using ordinary least squares without regularization, yet still yields a sparse and accurate model. The paper also provides explicit bounds for the bias and variance of its estimator, as well as the distribution of its normalized bias and variance. Our results demonstrate that non-regularized least squares achieves a model that is not only sparse but also accurate, with a bias and variance that satisfy specific inequalities. The paper's findings are verified through simulations and real-world applications, showcasing its relevance and usefulness. Recent studies propose utilizing Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HamNNs) for precise derivative acquisition, which can lead to enhanced performance in model training. However, a critical aspect to consider is the condition imposed by the Hamiltonian differential equation, specifically that the input signal must be smooth. This paper investigates the capability of HamNNs to learn precise derivatives from noisy data sets with varying levels of smoothness, also known as regularity. Our findings indicate that when the data has sufficient smoothness, both Hamiltonian Neural Networks and the standard Neural Network produce accurate derivatives. Nevertheless, when the data's smoothness decreases, the typical Neural Network yields suboptimal results, while HamNNs still delivers satisfactory performance. To mitigate this limitation, we introduce a new Hamiltonian Neural Network formulation, which can handle rough data by incorporating a noise-resistant component. This enhanced model outperforms the conventional HamNNs in all scenarios. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Almost all WSD systems rely on glossaries to provide general context about a word's possible meanings, which are often derived from online dictionaries like WordNet. However, these glossaries often cover all senses of a word but do not reflect the specific context of the target sentence. To enhance the performance of such systems, we propose a novel approach called Context-gloss to integrate both the general and specific contexts associated with a word. This approach involves incorporating both the dictionary-based gloss and the sentence-specific context when representing a word's possible meanings. To achieve this, we suggest a contextualized character-based model and a corresponding ranking algorithm to prioritize the words' representations that align with the context. Moreover, our method's capacity to integrate diverse sources of context also extends to other NLP tasks like sentiment analysis and sentence classification, thus offering a universally applicable framework. The enhanced word representations generated by our approach may also be useful in other NLP-related tasks. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. A key distinction between these theories is the location associated with the discovery of PTMs; since the experimental approach used here allows for varied design adjustments in edge coil placement and orientation without compromising data utility, this theoretical framework may be put to the test in the edge plasma measurement infrastructure of future tokamaks. A deeper comprehension of PTMs will likely contribute to the development of more robust devices against major disruptions during high plasma gain operations. Furthermore, this research implies that maintaining discovery capability in future tokamaks will require careful consideration of magnetic field sensing coil placement and orientation. A detailed discussion on the implications and benefits of this theoretical framework can be found in a companion paper. Our approach exceeds the limitations of traditional potential field methods by addressing local extrema and convergence issues. Moreover, it facilitates the creation of a comprehensive collision avoidance framework that can be used in various scenarios with linear and circular obstacles. Our results, verified through extensive simulations and actual experiments, demonstrate the efficacy and reliability of our collaborative collision avoidance technique. Our approach is exceptionally robust, able to handle priority assignments in a straightforward manner and is highly adaptable to accommodate the insertion of new robots at any time during ongoing operations. Introduction Potential field-based methods have long been the go-to solution for mobile robots to navigate around static and dynamic obstacles, avoid collisions, and achieve optimal paths due to their simplicity in implementation and computation. Despite these benefits, most traditional potential field approaches suffer from critical issues that significantly impede their performance in complex, real-world applications: the tendency of the robot to become stuck in local minima; and the inability to calculate optimal avoidance paths. This holds particularly true when implementing these solutions on actual robots, which are often plagued by the presence of friction, causing the robot to gravitate towards the very obstacle it is trying to avoid. In light of these challenges, researchers have resorted to collision avoidance schemes that prioritize reliability over optimality, notably receding horizon control, which has shown impressive results in various scenarios. Nevertheless, this state feedback approach has yet to be implemented in multi-robot settings due to the complexity involved. This research introduces a new method that incorporates dynamic vortex potential fields to provide a solution to the collision avoidance problem for a single mobile robot in the presence of other moving robots. This approach is then extended to multiple robots by applying the collision avoidance solution recursively, resulting in an optimal path being obtained for all robots involved. We have validated our approach through extensive simulations and actual experiments, which demonstrate its efficacy and robustness. The novel solution presented also addresses priority issues in a straightforward manner and has shown the ability to handle the addition of new robots during ongoing operations. Furthermore, this approach has been proven to be highly adaptable in scenarios involving linear and circular obstacles. In constant learning, a sequence of new machine learning tasks must be learned from data available only for the specific tasks at hand, without access to previous tasks. This is because there is no opportunity to revisit previous tasks or store the model used for each task. Continual learning therefore requires models that adapt to new data without compromising performance on data encountered earlier. One key challenge in continual learning is the problem of forgetting, which occurs when a model loses information learned from previous tasks. This is particularly true for visual classification tasks, where models must recognize a wide range of objects from limited data, a problem exacerbated by the fact that visual classification datasets are often composed of many classes, with each class represented by only a few examples. 

One approach to continual learning has been the development of neural network models that can learn from a sequence of tasks without the need for explicit control of model updates for each task. This has led to the creation of multi-task models that can learn from a variety of tasks simultaneously. However, such models often require extensive data available for all tasks at once, which is not a realistic assumption in continual learning scenarios.

Approximating two-player Nash equilibria in games with Lipschitz continuous payoffs has been investigated by extending the notion of Lipschitz continuity to a query complexity property of the function f, denoted as L_f. Previous works by Daskalov and Tsankov and Tsankov among others established sublinear L_f query complexities for finding Nash equilibria in various types of games including systems of parametrized linear inequalities, Gaussian games and isotonic games. However, the existing lower bound for these complexities in general games is linear. This paper raises that lower bound to an exponential one, indicating that finding Nash equilibria in games with Lipschitz continuous payoffs may not be significantly harder than verifying whether a given strategy profile constitutes an equilibrium under the same type of continuity. To achieve this higher lower bound, a new class of games was defined where the payoff functions have multiple layers of differentiation, thereby demonstrating an exponential L_f query complexity for finding Nash equilibria and an exponential increase in query complexity when searching for coarser granular equilibria, including coarse and very coarse equilibria. Moreover, a new class of coarse equilibrium-finding problems was introduced along with an associated problem definition that may be of interest on its own. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing the minimization of variance over the number of evaluated parameters. In line with this principle, our study demonstrates that a relatively small number of parameters can be optimally identified through 5-fold or 10-fold j-k CV across 5 or 10 subgroups, respectively. Moreover, the optimal parameters obtained via this approach exhibited superior generalizability when compared to the optimal solutions derived from conventional k-fold CV methods. Furthermore, our study showcases the applicability of the j-k CV method to a range of NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, sentiment detection, and grammaticality judgment, utilizing diverse models such as BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, DistilRoBERTa, SparkoBERT, and SparkRoBERTa. The source code for our experiments is openly available on GitHub, thereby enabling the exploration of this novel CV methodology across multiple NLP datasets and models. In conclusion, our study provides a compelling case for the adoption of the j-k CV framework to tackle machine learning's inherent variability (MLVAR), a pervasive issue affecting all machine learning applications. Moreover, we contend that successful resolution of this problem will facilitate the development of more robust and versatile machine learning models. Ultimately, our study on machine learning's inherent variability (MLVAR) may also be adapted for use with other complex optimization tasks that involve the interpretation of unstable performance estimates. In response to these challenges, our study proposes a novel statistical approach, designated as the j-k fold CV framework, which has been successfully evaluated across a range of NLP tasks and models.
