A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model that incorporates thermal and vibrational effects, simulating the reaction in various environments. Utilizing the Ehrenfest quantum dynamics method, our results revealed that non-equilibrium vibrational states in the reactant form influence the reaction's efficiency, with some vibrations enhancing the yield by a factor of ten in comparison to standard thermal equilibrium. Furthermore, we observed that particular vibrations with low energy gaps to the stable form can reach extremely high concentrations (n~17) in the reactant state, far exceeding those achievable in equilibrium configurations. These locations also coincide with areas under primary energy surfaces, indicating they function as an 'eye' that detects the available energy from the rhodopsin protein. The findings provide insight into the high sensitivity of visual systems, suggesting they may leverage the extensive range of non-equilibrium vibrational states in their molecular components to detect light. Additionally, our results demonstrate that utilizing parametric perturbations as an alternative to laser impulses can successfully drive the reaction in its stationary state, leading to rapid vibrationally mediated proton transfer. This process is normally associated with light activation and results in the conversion of alliopsin to bathorhodopsin in ~10 ps. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Our research is further reflected in an interactive
visualized repository where readers can explore and replicate our experiments. 
Ultimately, our experiments highlight the potential of deep learning models
for the predictive process area, however they also highlight the need for more
research in this exciting domain. Our research is supported by an affiliated
organization that provides access to an extensive dataset originating from
over 120 unique sources, spanning more than a decade. This dataset encompasses
over 1 million unique process instances originating from 28 different contexts
with multiple variables and over 300 unique event types with corresponding
attributes. This dataset is unique as it encompasses a variety of complex
processes with multiple activity types, different context conditions and varied
timing of case completion. This dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/duarteac/prediction-comparision. Our research is also currently being further
developed into a book chapter that is available at https://github.com/duarteac/pdp-book. This book chapter is a more
detailed extension of our research that is currently being reviewed for the 17th
International Conference on Distributed Open Source Techniques (DOT'23). This book
chapter is also a more in-depth development of previous research presented at
the 16th International Conference on Distributed Open Source Techniques (DOT'22).

A detailed simulation of a significant flare on the dwarf star AD Leo was achieved by modeling the atmospheric response to extreme ultraviolet radiation from the star's accretion layer.  Utilizing a general circulation model for the star's convective zone, researchers simulated the effects of high-energy radiation on their atmosphere above 1200 km above the stellar surface.  They found that this radiation caused the exosphere to expand and the accumulated gas above 2000 km to oscillate in a periodic manner, lasting 13.3 minutes, or almost exactly the duration of the extreme ultraviolet flash.  A key aspect of this simulation is the evidence it provides for the existence of a high-flow zone on AD Leo, specifically in the accretion layers, which produces near-ultraviolet continuum variations.  This specific phenomenon was observed during the 1985 April 12 great flare on AD Leo, and its underlying cause was initially misidentified as the effects of a high-flows on the star's convective zone, known as type II or III.  This incorrect explanation led to researchers proposing additional processes, yet none of these alternatives could accurately account for the 1200K surface layer's behavior during this event.  In contrast to these earlier findings, the more recent explanation for the flux increase during this event, first proposed in 2000, left unanswered the question of what drives the variations in the continuum, which is now provided by this new study.  This solution, which was based on data from the EUVE and IUE, showed that the variations in the continuum are caused by the interaction between the star's high-flow layers and its atmosphere above 1200 km, a process that is not limited to the stellar surface, known as type III, or in this case, type IV.  This simulation of the 1985 April 12 great flare on AD Leo, which displayed the highest intensity of any flare on this star, also produced evidence of a relationship between the increased mass flow during this event and its prolonged post-flare phase, which lasted 2.5 times the normal duration for this star. Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with adaptive forms that change layout based on input data. A major challenge in addressing this issue is the lack of a standardized visual template. Current deep learning solutions often struggle with this variability, as they typically rely on pre-trained models that focus on recognizing specific visual elements but neglect the overall form structure. This limitation prompts a new approach, one where the model is trained to recognize forms without preconceived notions of what the layout should look like. This approach is known as a template-free strategy. Our proposed template-free form recognition network is an innovative, layered model that learns to extract structural information from images of forms at multiple levels. It uses both spatial and sequential pattern recognition techniques to interpret visual data. By integrating a variational autoencoder, this model also learns to represent forms as meaningful code vectors. These code vectors not only facilitate comparison and classification of forms but also provide a compact, data-driven representation of the input images. Our experimental results show that this model performs exceptionally well on a diverse dataset of adaptive forms, achieving superior accuracy and code vector quality when compared to both a harmoniously integrated alternative model and several state-of-the-art template-based approaches. This model's versatility makes it an ideal solution for a broad range of real-world applications involving visual form recognition, such as identifying forms with numerical variables, and can serve as a foundation for the development of more sophisticated template-free model architectures. Its exceptional performance, coupled with its straightforward implementation and minimal reliance on pre-trained models, make it an attractive solution for both researchers and practitioners. The search for rare $\Sigma^+$ baryon decays with leptons, specifically $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, has yielded an apparent signal for this process at the LHCb experiment using 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected at 5.0 TeV center-of-mass energy. The observed count for this decay exceeds the forecast from the standard model by 4.3 standard deviations after taking into account various background sources. This result significantly surpasses the 3 standard deviation threshold required to consider it notable. To verify the rarity of these events, researchers employed an indirect approach by comparing $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$ to the expected rate for $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$, which has a established branching fraction. Following this method, the estimated standard model rate for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$ is $0.016 \pm 0.007$ in relative units to $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$, which is not statistically significant. This finding slightly reduces the impact of $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ discovery on existing searches for new physics but does not significantly alter existing constraints on theoretical models. Furthermore, a similar decay pattern $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma \gamma$ has no evidence for an existing standard model process but may be worth monitoring in the future. All findings provide further motivation for more intense research in these less explored standard model processes. Additionally, a more precise determination of $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$ at upgraded or next-generation particle accelerators could provide more accurate indirect detection of standard model anomalies.

The explosion of synthesized diffraction data brought by pixel detectors and automated data collection systems at x-ray facilities is staggering, producing an overwhelming amount of data in need of analysis. While specialized software can handle small to medium-sized datasets, the current challenge lies in processing large datasets of 10,000 to 100,000 individual scans, with each scan comprising 100 to 10,000 individual measurements. This processing bottleneck restricts the ability to conduct high-speed experiments under constant remote supervision. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that involves breaking down complex problems into manageable forms amenable to machine learning optimization, with a particular emphasis on data collected by varying an external parameter in a systematic and often random manner. By leveraging the unique features of synchrotron data and the capabilities of remote experimentation, we have developed an integrated suite of machine learning tools that can be used for real-time or post-hoc analysis of such datasets. These algorithms can be used in an automated high-speed data collection setup, integrated with the experimental setup's control system via APIs, allowing for real-time optimization and potential applications in biomolecular crystallography, Thomson scattering, and other high-throughput techniques. This integrated approach combines automated raw data analysis with real-time feedback, eliminating the delay typically associated with experimental data collection and potentially increasing the rate at which data is collected. This can result in up to 10 times faster data collection in certain scenarios. Moreover, this approach also enables the collection of statistical metrics during the experiment, such as standard deviations, which can be used to monitor the experiment's progress and make informed decisions about continuing the collection. By integrating machine learning with remote operation of large-scale user facilities, we can collect higher-quality datasets in a shorter amount of time, with the added benefit of being able to conduct experiments from anywhere with an internet connection. This has significant implications for the field of biomolecular crystallography, where the collection of high-quality datasets can be a time-consuming and challenging process. This technology also has the added benefit of enabling remote experimentation, which can increase the efficiency and productivity of experiments and reduce the costs associated with traveling to facilities. This is particularly important for small to medium-sized research institutions that may not have the resources to collect data in-house, as it allows them to collect high-quality datasets even if they don't have access to the necessary equipment. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian may seem beneficial, as it could exploit symmetry present in the problem Hamiltonian, but actually hindrances quantum annealing's effectiveness. These limitations can be overcome by introducing environmental interactions with the system, as demonstrated with an example of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. While quantum annealing fails when attempting to solve this model with a non-stoquastic driver, achieving solution with the help of decoherence results in a surprising finding that unstoquastic QA performs better than its stoquastic counterpart under certain conditions. Furthermore, this better performance can be understood through the lens of driver-problem overlap, a newly introduced concept, leading to the development of a general strategy for successful quantum annealing. This discovery unlocks possibilities for utilizing unstoquastic drivers in complex systems, potentially unlocking quantum annealing's full potential. However, it should be noted that environmental interactions can introduce errors, as they do not commute with the system's Hamiltonian, potentially limiting the approach's scalability. Lastly, a connection to the phenomenon of environmental assistance in quantum learning is established, as well as a discussion on the role that machine learning plays in both understanding and developing quantum annealing. Furthermore, a new direction for research is proposed, centered around the concept of environmental-assisted quantum annealing, as well as an examination of the broader implications of these findings on our understanding of quantum physics. We demonstrate that any Coxeter group possesses bi-automatic presentation, which is based on a distinguishing length function and a set of equitable relations. This conclusion is derived from a more general theorem stating that any group that has a length-quadratic finitely generated presentation and satisfies certain conditions is bi-automatic. Additional properties, including the capacity for torsion elements and a dense set of conjugacy classes, are shown to be bi-automatic as well. Furthermore, we prove that the group of upper-triangular matrices with integer entries and a systolic relation has a finite presentation and is therefore bi-automatic. From this, we deduce that the Coxeter group within such matrices is also bi-automatic. This result can be further applied to demonstrate automaticity in various situations. For instance, we show that the group of rational points on a sphere under hyperbolic metric-driven action is automatic. Lastly, we explore connections between our methods and previous work by R. Gilman in "Automatic groups: a further study". Moreover, we presemtly establish new criteria for automaticity, particularly in the case of finitely presented groups. This, combined with our main theorem, allows us to prove additional results on automaticity, such as the fact that the group of upper-triangular matrices with integer entries and a cyclic relation is automatic. Finally, we discuss various open questions related to the generalization of our main theorem. This research was initially discussed at the "Words and Combinatorics" seminar at the University of Vienna in 2019.

Humans naturally experience gait patterns known as 'normal gait', 'double support gait','single support gait', and 'brisk gait'. Brisk gait is characterized by longer strides and faster step rates compared to normal gait. Reciprocally, research suggests that increased cortical connectivity in the sensory-motor network is associated with brisk gait. However, the relationship between cortical connectivity, walking state, and step rate remains unclear. This study involves the collection of EEG data from 25 healthy adults while they walk on a treadmill at regular and accelerated speeds. Our novel approach identifies distinct patterns in electrocorticogram signals corresponding to different gait states and estimates step rates from these patterns. The results show that a method called 'k-neighbor weighting' is more effective in distinguishing between walking states and estimating step rates than traditional methods. Furthermore, our research reveals that multiple features of the brain's electrical activity are connected to walking state and step rate. Moreover, a crucial finding from this study is the observation that the brain's step rate estimation is precision-enhanced when brainer activity patterns are in sync with actual step rates. On the other hand, research on functional brain connectivity raises more questions than answers regarding the relationship between the brain and walking state/step rate. Lastly, our study demonstrates the potential of using cortical electrocorticogram signals to control a step rate feedback system based on a user's gait state. This feedback system is designed to provide auditory feedback that synchronizes with the user's actual step rate. In random systems, the scattering matrix describes how wave energy is scattered from its initial to a set of possible final forms. Recently, a method was developed to identify the most efficient paths for depositing energy into specific forms, even in complex systems. This technique involves breaking down the scattering matrix into a superposition of simple, non-interfering processes, known as its eigenchannel decomposition. Using this approach, we found a way to directly use these independent processes to calculate the total energy that could be deposited into a certain form, even if they cannot be mapped back from the energy deposition quantities. This new understanding and the ability to simulate and measure the energy deposition eigenchannels, provide a foundation for a broader'sum rule' that could describe most properties of scattering systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of these concepts to optimize energy deposition in two examples, with potential uses in areas such as laser technology and sound wave manipulation. Finally, we discuss how these ideas might be extended to other properties of scattering systems, like transmission or the scattering density of states. To that aim, we show that the energy deposition sum rule can be expressed in terms of the scattering matrix's eigenchannels and a new quantity, the 'density of paths', which we also measure and simulate in our experiments. This rule is a generalization of a previous formula for uniform systems and could be used to study systems that scatter different forms of energy, like sound waves or electromagnetic waves. Additionally, we found a relationship between the density of paths and another quantity, known as the localization length, which could provide insight into how the dimensionality of a system affects its scattering behavior. Lastly, we explore how to modify a system in order to increase its 'communication' with different forms of wave energy, and we discuss some possible ways to experimentally measure the energy deposition eigenchannels and density of paths. This involves using a new approach based on the eigenchannels of the scattering matrix, rather than old methods that relied on interfering paths. This could also lead to a better understanding of how to manipulate and control the scattering of different wave forms in various types of systems. Lastly, we discuss some potential future directions for this line of research. This could involve studying systems that scatter different forms of energy, like sound waves or electromagnetic waves, or looking at how the density of paths changes in different types of system dimensions. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on quantum error correction, which is typically achieved through code-driven recovery processes. Conventionally, quantum error correction codes are executed using classical control systems, but the incorporation of continuous-variable coders offers a coding alternative that simplifies the decoding process, transforming it into a continuous measurement problem. This shift raises the potential for learning-encoded relationships through reinforcement learning, a previously unexplored approach to coders. We introduce the concept of continuous-learning coders and assess its applicability and performance, particularly focusing on the Walsh-Hamming code, a promising candidate for quantum error correction. Simulation results demonstrate the potential of continuous-learning coders to surpass conventional performance standards, especially under certain types of noise conditions. Furthermore, this concept lays the foundation for future exploration of learning-encoded relationships to be extended to other quantum error correction codes, such as topological codes, by leveraging the continuous-learning coder framework. We also discuss the scope for coding research to explore new coders that combine learning-driven and fault-tolerant properties, enabling the development of more adaptable quantum computing systems. This vision for the future of quantum computing is centered on the idea that learning coders will be an essential element, providing a critical opportunity for interdisciplinary research between quantum information sciences and machine learning. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. The hadron $p_T$ spectrum also displays greater than $p$$+$$p$ scaling at large radii, and hadron types differ in their within-medium interactions as inferred from global $p_T$ conservation. These findings demonstrate that the medium's interaction with hadrons is not merely elastic, but also includes non-perturbative components, such as hadron splitting and the creation of hadron pairs. Additionally, the ratio of hadron pairs to single hadrons at small angles and high hadron $p_T$ exceeds $p$$+$$p$ collisions, indicating additional medium effects. A detailed understanding of these processes requires precise study of direct photon-hadron correlations. Consequently, the PHENIX detector's upgraded jetfinder now incorporates a direct photon-hadron component, allowing for the simultaneous investigation of jet and direct photon phenomena in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au collisions from 2015. Initial results for zero-degree hadron calorimeter photons show that hadron production around the jet axis is suppressed in Au$+$Au compared to $p$$+$$p$, and the hadron $p_T$ spectrum exceeds $p$$+$$p$ scaling at large distances from the beam pipe. Furthermore, hadron types exhibit distinct within-medium interactions as inferred from global $p_T$ conservation. These findings demonstrate that the medium's interaction with hadrons is not merely elastic but also non-perturbative, involving hadron splitting and the creation of hadron pairs. This approach, however, may introduce variability in network performance, masking its effects on application scalability through increased noise. To examine the underlying causes and effects of this phenomenon, this paper presents a holistic noise-catalyzing model that captures the unpredictable behavior of both application tasks and virtualized network components. Through this model, we uncover the implications of network variability on scalability, and its associated metrics such as stationarity, conditioning, and the impact of application task distributions. Our findings, validated by both simulation and real-world data, reveal that network variability can significantly impede the scalability of applications, reducing their capacity for scale-out and even reversing the benefits of doing so in some cases. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive scaling algorithm that tackles the issues of stationarity and conditioning, and demonstrate its superior performance in achieving optimized scalability across various application workloads. This algorithmic solution can be employed by autonomous services to optimize their scalability across noisy multi-tenant clouds. Additionally, we introduce the CloudNoise dataset, a comprehensive collection of network performance data from real-world cloud deployments, along with a related set of metrics and visualization techniques that facilitate the exploration and characterization of noisy network behavior. This dataset, along with our proposed scalable application framework, can aid in developing more effective and resilient cloud applications capable of withstanding the variability inherent in cloud environments. This variability poses significant challenges to the development of cloud applications, limiting their potential for success. Therefore, a deeper understanding of the unique characteristics of cloud noise, along with the creation of tailored, noisy-aware application designs is essential to unlocking the full potential of cloud computing. This is where our adaptive scaling algorithm and the CloudNoise dataset come into play, providing a solution to the scalability challenges posed by network variability in cloud computing. A previously theoretical concept involving a droplet fan generated by electrohydrodynamic forces in a gas-phase aerosol has been successfully demonstrated experimentally. The fan, composed of up to 10,000 droplets, was created through the electrohydrodynamic force field and its behavior was captured using a combination of high-speed imaging and laser-induced fluorescence. Our findings show that the fan exhibits a consistent and droplet-number-dependent structure, with droplets arranged in a symmetric and orderly manner. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fan can be used to concentrate fluorescent dye within the aerosol, beyond what could be achieved with conventional means. This innovation has the potential to enhance the concentration of droplets or particles within an aerosol, a challenge often encountered in various experimental applications. Building upon this success, we propose a range of applications where a droplet fan could offer advantages in both fundamental and applied research. Our approach also raises the possibility of creating complex, interconnected droplet networks within an aerosol environment. With many phenomena involving multiple droplets remaining poorly understood, the ability to construct complex droplet assemblies could provide a pathway for further exploration and insight. With its versatility, our method could be adapted for use in both high-speed and temperature-controlled experiments, further expanding the possibilities for droplet fan research and its various applications. Effective information navigation relies on more than just basic fact-checking skills. To move forward, we need to create a more advanced understanding of text that can handle complex elements like negation. To contribute to this effort, we present CONDAQA, a pioneering English dataset of 5,728 questions, designed to evaluate a text's negative information and assess the reasoning required to understand the original context. CONDAQA covers a broad range of topics and is distinctive in its use of actual quiz answers from a knowledge base, which poses challenges for both traditional IR systems and cutting-edge models like BART and ALBERT. Our evaluation shows that current state-of-the-art models still have much to learn about handling negation and other context - a skill that we demonstrate machines can master with proper training on CONDAQA. Our findings also indicate that significant performance gains can be achieved through additional fine-tuning on a diverse set of datasets that target a range of context types. Last but not least, we introduce Fuze, a novel attention-based architecture that excels in responding to CONDAQA questions surpassing all existing models and achieving near-human performance. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phase of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and is utilized for solving computational issues, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes and is employed to investigate the ensuing non-equilibrium dynamics. This study offers insight into the relationship between quantum annealing and quenching, providing a new means of interval estimation in the process. Furthermore, the proposed interval estimation method is found to yield superior results when compared to other approaches in the exact cover problem, a more intricate challenge than the Ising model. When designing a software system, a choice must be made about the testing method - structured testing or systematic testing. Structured testing involves selecting test cases from a coverage criteria such as white-box or black-box approaches, whereas systematic testing entails picking test cases via random chance. We propose an approach that chooses test cases via a method called singular value decomposition, or SVD. By calculating the distance between each test case and the desired target, or fault scenario, we can prioritize test cases with the greatest variation in results. This process is both objective and automatic in nature. We've taken this approach and integrated it with the parallel version of the algorithm called Parallel Quick Fix, or PQF, to see if it yields a more efficient and effective means of selecting test cases. Our findings suggest that the SVD method outperforms the traditional approach in almost every aspect, especially when there's a large number of test cases to choose from. Furthermore, the SVD-PQF hybrid method demonstrates superior performance in terms of solution quality when compared to the traditional PQF algorithm. We've also established the theoretical limits of the SVD-PQF method and outline the ingredients for a successful implementation of this approach in other software testing applications. By utilizing a dataset comprised of 1200 test cases and 25 fault scenarios, we validated the efficacy of the SVD-PQF method, or SDVPQF for short, and concluded that it yields the optimal solution in a vast majority of cases, or about 78%. We've implemented the SDVPF algorithm in a real-world setting at IBM and observed a significant reduction in testing time of up to 90%. Our study has provided a valuable framework for addressing other complex, real-world challenges, such as determining the number of test cases to select, or whether to settle for a suboptimal solution in a timely manner. We've explored alternative approaches to solve these issues, including fixed-size SDVPF, or FSSDV, and quasi-SDVPF, or QSDDV, respectively. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external semantic information. Presently, most existing approaches primarily utilize pre-trained models with vast amounts of data, relying on their inherent semantic knowledge to generate responses. These approaches, however, fail to leverage tailored semantic-related insights, which can facilitate careful and precise reasoning to address challenging questions. This paper introduces a novel framework that allows for the incorporation of semantic-related insights in the form of additional textual evidence. These insights can guide the coarse initial predictions made by models, such as BERT, to ensure they are accurate and relevant. By incorporating structured semantic relations from WordNet, this framework enables the creation of contextual prompts that can seek careful and precise insights from these models. The results of our experiments demonstrate notable improvements in achieving correct answers on the CommonsenseQA dataset when using this framework. Moreover, our approach is especially effective at avoiding the inclusion of irrelevant information in answers, as evidenced by the significant reduction in F-score for incorrect answers. Additionally, our approach is found to be generally applicable across various models and even outperforms the performance of finer-grained multiple-choice answers on the same dataset. These findings suggest that carefully incorporating semantic-related insights can significantly enhance the performance of open-domain commonsense question-answering tasks. This approach is made available as part of the CoQaQA toolkit, an open-source code repository provided with this paper. By introducing a novel evaluation metric that assesses the quality of textual evidence, we also provide a complementary version of this toolkit as well as the dataset created with the framework, both of which are made available through the code repository. This dataset comprises the textual evidence created with WordNet and the resulting CommonsenseQA dataset, which combines 4500 questions with the corresponding contextual prompts and multiple-choice answers in the form of WordNet concepts. This combination of question types, along with the inclusion of the context from the prompt, leads to a notable improvement in performance when using this dataset with models that can process this additional context. However, it should be noted that the current version of this paper focuses solely on the development of the CoQaQA framework and associated tools. Research indicates that individuals within the criminal justice system, who have not yet been found guilty or pleaded guilty, experience higher rates of poor mental health compared to the broader population. This study analyzes the impact of mandatory mental health therapy on these individuals within the German criminal justice system. Participants were randomly assigned to either the control group, which consisted of individuals who received standard treatment, or the treatment group, which consisted of individuals who received eight sessions of psychosocial therapy in addition to standard treatment. The study's primary metric for assessing the treatment's effectiveness was the difference in symptom severity before and after treatment. The analysis revealed a statistically significant reduction in symptom severity among treatment group participants, with an average decrease of 31% compared to 11% in the control group. Additionally, re-arrest rates within three years following release from custody were lower among treatment group participants by an absolute 12 percentage points, although this finding was not statistically significant. Notably, the treatment's benefits extended to subgroups with the most severe mental health issues and those who had prior convictions. This research provides initial evidence on the effectiveness of mandatory mental health therapy within the criminal justice system and suggests it may be an valuable tool in reducing recidivism rates. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across language boundaries, for example using a pre-trained model for low-resource languages from a related high-resource language. We explored this approach for 10 languages within the Cross-Lingual ASR Transfer (CLASRT) dataset, specifically looking at how it applies to zero-shot, few-shot, and one-shot learning scenarios. We discovered smaller models pre-trained on general data resulted in better performance compared to larger models, and fine-tuning on a single sentence significantly enhanced outcomes. Ultimately, our final findings reveal impressive results, including a notable 50% reduction in error rate in a zero-shot Portuguese task from 21.39% to 10.57%. We also found that when no data from the target language is available, pre-training on untranscribed data can be beneficial. We hope these results influence future CLASR research to focus on untranscribed data availability, along with related issues such as data quality and availability across languages. We anticipate future breakthroughs resulting from the exploration of unsupervised and low-shot learning strategies, along with novel pre-training objectives, to be crucial in the development of next-generation neural network-based ASR systems. The task of allocating essential or preferred items to self-interested and rational agents, where the items' value cannot be split, is a well-known and complex problem in economics and computer science. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new method for assigning items without the requirement for full flexibility in division. Our approach ensures the existence of equilibrium outcomes that are computationally manageable and, crucially, guarantees the existence of fair solutions within the spectrum of computationally feasible alternatives. Building on this foundation, we explore two expanded settings: first, where the ability to split items is limited to their specific parts; second, where the ability to split items is unrestricted. For the first of these expanded settings, we develop an efficient method for obtaining computationally feasible and fair solutions. For the second, where the ability to split items is unrestricted, we show the existence of computationally feasible and fair solutions for specific classes of agents, but find that this requires more restrictive assumptions about the agents' values. Our research on the second expanded setting, where the ability to split items is unrestricted, yields new insights into the fundamental challenges of allocating items to self-interested agents, but the results do not lead to the development of computationally feasible and fair solutions. Finally, we explore an alternative formulation of item allocation, called the 'one-way combinatorial auction', which allows for the allocation of items that can be split in combination, but not on their own, and find that this setting can be reduced to an efficient fair solution. Building on this, we extend our approach to an expanded setting for the combinatorial auction, where the ability to split items is unrestricted, and develop an efficient method for obtaining computationally feasible and fair solutions. This research provides novel solutions to fundamental challenges in economics and computer science. The developed methods can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as scheduling, logistics, and resource allocation in computing and communication systems. We investigate the occurrences of radio frequency sources within 19 Galactic globular clusters using the MAVERIC dataset from the VLA. Upon examining 78 candidate radio sources within a half degree of the cluster cores, we determine their spectral types and identify 27 contaminants, leaving 51 sources associated with the clusters. By modeling the frequency spectra of 34 cluster sources, we find 23 of them exhibit millisecond pulsar characteristics, 7 are consistent with neutron star binaries, and the remaining 5 are classified as radio bursts or unidentified. Our analysis indicates that the majority of detected radio sources within these clusters remain unaccounted for, revealing a significant discrepancy in the count of detected sources (35) in comparison to the total estimated population (153). This shortfall is attributed to the prevalence of intermediate mass black holes found at the centers of globular clusters. A correlation between the cluster's compact object population and the density of radio sources within those clusters also exists, supporting the idea that the previously unmapped frequency range may provide insight into the cluster's compact object population density. A further examination of the detected radio sources within the Large Magellanic Cloud does not reveal any evidence of hidden black holes. Nevertheless, the low detected ratio of black holes to white dwarfs in the LMC suggests that the abundance of black holes in the MAVERIC cluster sample may be significantly higher than previously estimated, thus offering a potential explanation for the numerous unexplained radio sources within those clusters. A more in-depth analysis of the detected radio sources and their host clusters is also presented, along with a discussion on the implications of these findings in relation to the prevalence of black holes in the Galactic halo. Ultimately, this study highlights the significance of multi-frequency research in the context of radio frequency source origins within globular clusters. A critique of the theoretical black hole formation model is also presented in this study's conclusion, along with a discussion of several alternative explanations for the prevalence of radio frequency sources within these clusters. Offline learning for multiple agents learning together from each other's historical interactions is crucial for developing practical applications involving multiple actors by leveraging existing data. However, offline learning for multi-agent systems is complicated by issues of relying on suboptimal experiences from other agents and the difficulty of identifying the best actions to learn from existing trajectories. This paper introduces an offline learning framework called Learning From Good Paths (LFGP) that addresses these challenges by defining a series of persistent policies that can be learned from each other's most effective experiences, thus allowing for better performance from individual agents and better cooperation between them, as verified through multiple assessment scenarios. The proposed approach also offers a solution to a critical challenge in offline multi-agent policy evaluation and can be integrated with optimization-based behavior improvement. Furthermore, LFGP is applicable to various types of multi-agent scenarios and is particularly effective in scenarios that are highly collaborative, as shown through experiments on various games and scenarios. Megavoltage imaging is a technique that provides detailed information about body structures, particularly useful in obesity and sclerodermia treatments. However, these images lack color and are poorly lit, making them difficult to align with standard low-voltage images obtained through CT scans or other processes. This issue hinders the integration of megavoltage images with treatment plans created using low-voltage images, forcing practitioners to skip using certain images in the alignment process.

To address this challenge, we developed a novel approach for aligning 2D/3D megavoltage images using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). This method involves training two separate CNNs to identify corresponding tissue types and boundary features in megavoltage images, with one network handling 2D images and the other 3D images. Once trained, the two CNNs work together to map low-voltage images to corresponding megavoltage images, with their combined output used for final alignment.

Our results show that this technique achieves highly accurate alignments, with tests using real patient images showing an average alignment error of just 3.8 mm when assessed by three experienced medical physicists and radiation therapists. This method is not only more accurate than existing techniques but also significantly faster, taking only a few seconds to execute on a standard GPU. To facilitate adoption, we've created a ready-to-use implementation of this method available on GitHub under an open-source license. This technique has the potential to integrate megavoltage images with treatment plans created using low-voltage images, opening up more flexible treatment options for patients. Furthermore, this method can be adapted for use with other low- to high-contrast image alignment applications. In contrast, we find that in the toric code model of quantum error correction, single-qubit rotations around the y-axis can be achieved through a multi-qubit gate based on any number of qubits, while rotations around the x and z axes cannot be achieved with these multi-qubit gates. Additionally, we determine the requirements for achieving the x-rotations and find that achieving one x-rotation requires a highly entangled state across all qubits in a resource code, but that this does not significantly impact threshold error rates when x-rotation gates are repeatedly applied across different qubits. Furthermore, we find that two-qubit gates can be used to create large-scale unitaries equivalent to the tensor product of single-qubit unitaries, but this relies on stable two-qubit gates and cannot be achieved with multi-qubit gates when there are unmeasured errors, significantly improving the requirement for two-qubit gates being nearly perfect. Lastly, we analyze various combinations of single-qubit y-rotations that can be achieved with either two-qubit gates or multi-qubit gates, finding that achieving those that are even powers can be done reliably with multi-qubit gates, but this does not hold for odd-powered rotations. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Numerical results demonstrate the codebook's efficiency yields substantial gains in data transfer rates. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable to various channel conditions and does not require knowledge of statistics at the base station. By comparing the approximate solution to the Bondi solution, we derive an inequality that sets a limit on the rate of mass change within the Bondi equation. This derived inequality can be expressed in terms of the Bondi mass scale, which represents the overall mass variation of a region of space. The Bondi mass scale is found to be directly proportional to the square of the Bondi radius and the rate of expansion of the universe. In the context of the standard Big Bang model, this leads to a constraint on the rate of mass change at any given scale, which is determined by the curvature of the universe. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
Existing text-based games are typically designed with limited complexity, allowing simulation rates of up to 10,000 actions per second.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, allowing for simulation speeds of over one million actions per second on a single CPU core.
We demonstrate the feasibility of creating sophisticated text-based games with intricate storylines and realistic dialogue at rates exceeding 200,000 actions per second, and showcase how incorporating human-like narration can be achieved with speeds of up to 200,000 strings per second.
Our findings indicate that current robotic agents struggle to perform optimally in TextWorldExpress across all measures, despite excelling in individual aspects. 
Our research provides a superior framework for assessing the practical problem-solving abilities of virtual agents in real-world scenarios. 
We invite the community to participate in an open challenge for enhancing the TextWorldExpress games through the TextWorldExpress Competition contest, and offer the TextWorldExpress Framework as a free resource for testing the efficacy of artificial agents. 
Our research is also introduced as an upgraded version of the game challenges presented at the 2018 TextWorld Workshop, and is now available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. 
TextWorldExpress has already been used in conjunction with learning agents by several researchers, and we are proud to have contributed to the development of multiple successful PhD theses. 
Our research has also given rise to several new challenges, such as the creation of more intricate narrative structures in text-based games, which we have made available on GitHub under the name of TwGame Planning. 
This new challenge involves defining the rules for generating TwGame stories that can be simulated at rates of over one million actions per second, and has the potential to advance the field of artificial intelligence through the development of more realistic human-like narration. 
We have presented initial findings on TwGame Planning at the 2020 Conference of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence, and a more in-depth analysis will be presented in an upcoming future publication. 
We have also explored extending the TextWorldExpress Challenge to include human participants, and have gathered an initial set of statistics on the performance of state-of-the-art robotic agents in comparison to human players, which will be a topic of discussion in our future research report.

In deep learning applications, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are widely employed for sequential data analysis. Nevertheless, their extensive use in video identification is hindered by the computational requirements and memory constraints of modern computing systems. To address this challenge, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to enhance the performance of LSTM networks on video identification tasks. A novel hardware framework based on the Hierarchical Tucker (HT) tensor decomposition of input video data is also presented. Through the application of HT tensor decomposition, the memory needs for LSTMs are significantly reduced, alongside a decline of approximately 10 times in computational operations. When applied to the GMU Video Identification Dataset, this integrated approach yields a 20% enhancement in accuracy and a 5x improvement in energy efficiency when compared to the baseline system. Furthermore, a 32-million-weights LSTM model demonstrates superior performance over simpler models comprising 11 million weights, achieving an overall accuracy of 88.5% for the easy-classification subset of the dataset. This research provides a framework for enhancing the performance of LSTM networks on video identification tasks through the incorporation of HT tensor decomposition. Nonetheless, the optimization of LSTM networks with this decomposition remains an unresolved issue. To address this challenge, this research decomposes only the input video data into the HT tensor format, whereas future studies could explore the application of this decomposition to output and hidden state vectors. Additionally, further research is needed to fully integrate the decomposed data into the LSTM framework and the proposed hardware accelerator. Nonetheless, the results presented in this paper demonstrate the efficacy of HT tensor decomposition as an unstructured memory access pattern and the benefits derived from the accelerated computation of compressed data. As such, this research is anticipated to contribute positively to the advancement of low-power LSTM networks. Nevertheless, the substantial computational requirements and memory constraints of modern computing systems often hinder the extensive use of LSTMs in these settings. To address this challenge, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware centered around the HT tensor decomposition of input data. Mobile agents require robust localization methods that rely on internal sensors such as visual and inertial data. We present an innovative external memory attention model, called EMA-VIO, for real-time visual-inertial localization across various environments. Despite this challenge, current information systems are designed to handle vast amounts of data, but they often lack the capability to efficiently collect relevant information from various sources about specific topics. This proposed new information system, called Federated Selective Collection for Knowledge Amalgamation (FeSCoKA), addresses this shortcoming by enabling the retrieval of specific documents from a vast pool of information, across which which users can then browse and interact. This new system complements traditional document retrieval systems by focusing on collecting sets of documents rather than individual documents. To achieve this, FeSCoKA is a hybrid approach that combines natural language processing, machine learning, and expert input to identify the most important concepts related to a given topic, and then uses these concepts to select a diverse set of relevant papers. By providing a flexible interface for users to modify the concept graph used for selection, FeSCoKA also enables the adaptation of the collected set of papers to their specific needs. This new system has several key benefits, including the ability to handle a broad range of domains and topics through the use of pre-trained natural language models, reducing the risk of bias through the incorporation of multiple sources of expertise, and empowering users to take full control of the collection process. Approximately twenty years ago, a theoretical framework known as the neural map theory began to take shape, suggesting that the brain's spatial navigation capabilities are driven by grid networks within the medial entorhinal cortex. This hypothetical grid framework was initially supported by computational models, but subsequent experimental discoveries have significantly advanced our understanding of grid neurons. A multitude of studies on rodents has yielded a wealth of information regarding grid neurons' functional characteristics, including the periodic structure of their preferred locations within a environment, the flexibility of their periodicity across different environments, and the dynamics of their periodic responses over time. This survey aims to present an overview of the current scientific knowledge on grid neurons, their implied grid cells, and the potential underlying mechanisms, as well as the related network aspects of the neural map theory, particularly focusing on the grid cell aspect. Some of the key drivers behind the variety of grid neuron phenomena have been identified through direct observation and quantitative analysis of recent data, often with the aid of computational modeling. This database can serve as a valuable resource for computational models focusing on grid neurons. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. This research explores the impact of anti-solar differential rotation on solar-type dynamos during the main sequence, considering possible magnetic cycles induced by this differential rotation pattern. By incorporating turbulence simulations and applying the α-$Ω$ dynamo approach, this study discovers that anti-solar differential rotation can generate a non-axisymmetric poloidal magnetic field, potentially explaining magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars. However, this solution is unstable and characterized by an increase in toroidal flux over time, which could be restrained by magnetic braking. The findings of this research have implications for the rotation patterns of slowly rotating solar-type stars, potentially identifying them as magnetic white-light stars. Furthermore, this study suggests that anti-solar differential rotation may become prevalent in the interior of these stars at sufficiently low rotational velocities. The outcomes of this research are applicable to stars retiring from their rapid braking phase and entering a state of rotational stability, characteristic of their slowly decaying oscillations and potential magnetic cycles. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a precise formula for the distinguishability duration. For non-unitary dynamics described by a decay Hamiltonian, we establish an upper bound for the distinguishability duration in relation to the system's relaxation time. Furthermore, we identify two new, asymmetry-specific monotones of the density matrix, derive their maximum rates of change for any qubit state, and demonstrate that these monotones reach their supremum values at uniform states. Additionally, we find that the minimum time to reach a distinguishable state is directly proportional to these monotone rates of change. Notably, this proportionality holds for both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. We also derive the optimal control strategies for reaching a distinguishable state along the maximum monotone rates of change, and these strategies involve either a unitary diagonal Hamiltonian or a decay Hamiltonian with a specific decay operator. We demonstrate our findings with specific examples of unitary and non-unitary dynamics. Furthermore, we observe that the proposed bounds for the distinguishability duration are more restrictive than the established bounds based on the von Neumann entropy. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our results in the context of quantum speed limits and the optimization of unitary control. Additionally, we provide an expanded discussion on the generalizing our results to multiple qubit systems. Finally, we conclude by summarizing our key contributions and outcomes.

This work explores possible reasons for the present state of Venus's atmosphere. We suggest that the high surface temperature and pressure, coupled with abundant CO and HCO+ gases, indicate water vapor played a crucial role in the planet's atmospheric development. Composed primarily of CO2, its initial atmosphere could have been generated through carbon-rich volatile delivery mechanisms. However, the excessive surface temperature ultimately led to extensive water vaporization, leading to a cycle of water loss that has persisted, resulting in the HCO+ gases we observe today. This process has been fueled by the planet's minimal magnetic field and intense radiation from the Sun. Furthermore, we propose that the substantial amounts of sulfuric acid present in Venus's atmosphere may actually be detrimental to chemical reactions that could break down water vapor, preventing a more extensive loss of water through atmospheric processes. This theory may have implications for the habitability of planets within the Goldilocks Zone, as even seemingly ideal conditions can be compromised by unseen atmospheric processes. Lastly, this model highlights the intricate relationships within the atmospheric development of complex planetary systems, underscoring the importance of interdisciplinary study in astrophysics and planetary science. Key factors influencing the evolution of Venus's atmosphere also reside at the intersection of astrobiology and exoplanetary research, as they set the stage for the environment necessary for life to thrive on other worlds. High-resolution figures in the supporting online material depict the water vapor depletion process, the redox state of Venus's core, and the atmospheric chemistry of sulfuric acid, among other visual representations of our findings. The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the comprehensive understanding of alterations in cellular organizations within tissues. Advances in digital pathology have made it possible to examine tissues at a hierarchical level, from the whole organ down to individual cells. Existing approaches to cancer research often focus solely on the cellular level, overlooking the complex, hierarchically structured networks of cells within tissues. To bridge this knowledge gap, our proposed framework, HierNet, leverages deep learning techniques to create hierarchical network representations of tissues. By progressively refining representations at successive scales, HierNet produces a series of successively more detailed and localized density maps that capture the intricate relationships among structures at each scale. We validated HierNet through various applications in the context of cancer research, including the detection and classification of cells, identification of tissue patterns, and prediction of mortality rates based on tissue architecture. Our results demonstrate that HierNet's flexible, multi-scale approach outperforms existing methods in multiple tasks. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that HierNet's learned representations not only aid in cancer diagnosis but also provide valuable insights into the complex interactions within tissues. We made HierNet's source code and data sets available for public access. As cancer research often prioritizes the whole over its individual parts, our work highlights the importance of examining the intricate networks within tissues. We anticipate that HierNet's unique blend of precision and interpretability will become a standard in the development of subsequent computer-assisted cancer diagnosis tools. Numerical simulations relying on the Fast Multipole Method face a distortion error indigenous to their approach, which significantly hinders their utilization in simulations preserving angular momentum. This paper presents an algorithmic refinement of the FMM, transforming it into a method suitable for simulations requiring angular momentum preservation. We introduce boundary extension techniques based on the interaction matrix, a novel way to calculate boundary-based translation matrices, and a format adjustment for rotation matrices in the context of the light cone formulation. These innovations enable us to derive an extended Hamiltonian map feasible for implementing in time-integrated numerical schemes such as the Stormer-Versenburger method. We validate our preserved FMM by comparing it against an exact N-body simulation in a one-dimensional setup and also present simulations of the ensemble distribution resulting from the preserved FMM's application. These findings provide insight into the role of initial conditions and system size in determining the outcome of FMM-based simulations. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of applying this refined FMM to three-dimensional simulations following the advice of Barnes & Hut in formatting the pair-wise interaction list. This revised format prevents cross-talk between particles in the evaluation of their motion, thus allowing the implementation of the preserved FMM. We demonstrate the feasibility of this three-dimensional variant by simulating the evolution of a harmonic potential in one dimension, an operation not previously feasible with standard FMM. These developments make it feasible to execute the preserved FMM on three-dimensional simulations requiring the conservation of angular momentum. We anticipate this refinement to contribute positively to the advancement of computational astrophysics. Furthermore, we invite the broader scientific community to collaborate with us on the further development of this computational method. One method to enhance the scale and diversity of available data is to segment comparable anatomical structures across similar domains, which is what this paper proposes to accomplish through the application of contrastive learning in cross-domain segmentation. A novel model based on a contrastive semi-supervised learning framework is introduced, combining the use of pre-trained models, contrastive learning, and entropy-based regularization. The proposed framework's effectiveness is demonstrated across three segmentation tasks on three distinct domains, with the results showing it outperforms the pre-trained model and existing SSL approaches. However, these plasmas can introduce significant additional losses due to the wide spectral width of the ionized states. A different, magnetized plasma environment can alter the energy levels of the atoms, shifting them out of alignment with the laser's frequency and reducing interelectronic variations. This study shows that such a plasma can not only withstand extremely high laser intensities and broaden the refractive index with minimal additional loss but also amplify a wide range of frequencies beyond those of the core laser component. The amplified sidebands can also exhibit very high peak powers, potentially enabling new possibilities for the production of ultra-intense, ultra-short pulses. The theoretical model used in this research can support multi-petawatt pulse amplification and it is believed that this novel approach to pulse amplification could be applicable to various contexts, including astrophysical events involving intense laser-like phenomena. Furthermore, this discovery may facilitate the development of novel methods for generating ultra-short, ultra-intense laser pulses through the interaction of magnetized plasmas and intense laser beams. Rank metric (RM) error correction can be applied to compensate for faulty memory accesses in data storage systems, improving system reliability. A new decoding concept, known as decoding under the null space or DecNS, has been proposed to enhance the effectiveness of RM error correction. Rather than rejecting corrupted data, DecNS enables the recovery of stored information even after it has passed through a faulty memory access, whose impact can be described by a matrix with a specific null space. By utilizing DecNS for each possible combination of null spaces associated with a given rank, the storage capacity of a data storage system can be increased by approximately one bit per storage location. This decoding approach can also be combined with conventional RM decoding methods to further improve its performance. Our findings demonstrate that DecNS outperforms conventional RM decoding techniques by up to 300% in certain scenarios. Moreover, DecNS can be implemented using a variant of the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm, optimizing its computational complexity and making it suitable for practical application in data storage systems. Additionally, our research introduces two practical variants of DecNS, including DecNS with a limited number of trials and DecNS with a predefined null space, to balance the trade-off between error correction performance and computational complexity. These variants can also be incorporated into conventional RM codes to further improve their performance. Our conclusions on DecNS are complemented by an innovative application of source coding, specifically lattice trellis weighted cumulative average (LTWCA), which leverages DecNS-eligible data storage locations to lexicographically prioritize the reconstruction of original data from corrupted memory accesses. This new LTWCA strategy can be integrated with DecNS to further enhance the effectiveness of faulty memory access compensation. Our theoretical analysis and extensive simulations with various data storage configurations and faulty memory access scenarios provide a comprehensive evaluation of DecNS and its applications. Our research on DecNS and its variants has significant implications for the design of data storage systems, providing a framework for optimizing system storage capacity, comprehensively balancing the trade-off between error correction performance and computational complexity. Our conclusions on DecNS and its applications serve as a reference for further research into this decoding concept and its extensions in the broader context of coding theory. Our simulations have been carried out using up to 64 processors on a Dell PowerEdge R730 server, with each processor operating at 2.40 GHz. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however, delensing is an essential step in achieving this accuracy and it introduces a complex factor in modeling and analysis processes. The standard approach to delensing relies on the estimation of the primordial power spectrum from a reconstructed lensing potential, but this method's efficiency decreases with an increase in the level of primordial tensor fluctuations, which are modeled as a Gaussian random field in this study. To improve delensing performance and make the process more robust to various primordial tensor fluctuations, we trained and tested a neural network on simulated data from a model that includes Gaussian primordial tensor fluctuations - the results showed the delensing estimator's bias remains well within the $r$-forecast precision threshold of 0.01 when trained on various models including those with high primordial tensor fluctuations. Additionally, a comparison with a more conservative approach that uses a minimum variance estimator showed the neural network's delensing performance is up to 5 times better on small scales. This improves the overall estimation of $r$ by about a factor of 2 when combining all scales. Moreover, the variance of the delensing estimator is shown to be more robust to various primordial tensor fluctuations when using the neural network method. This includes a significant improvement in the low signal-to-noise region, which is usually the most challenging one. We also found that the neural network's performance is robust to different configurations and various choices of hyperparameters. This new delensing estimator offers a more robust approach to tackling the challenges posed by primordial tensor fluctuations and will likely be a vital component in the analysis of future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background. This is especially true when measuring the primordial tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ below the level of 0.01. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, Nukmer. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also compared our numerical results with existing analytical solutions. A major constraint in the development and testing of NLP models is the high cost of manually labeling data.  For document extraction models, this typically involves annotating individual fields within a variety of different template-based document types.  While existing methods can efficiently scale to handle a broad category of documents, such as various invoice styles, they can quickly become expensive when applied to a single complex document type.  Existing research has demonstrated that models trained on a wide range of visual classification tasks can be trained with minimal labeled data, but this typically requires a large dataset of labeled data on individual documents.  This research takes a more radical approach, reducing the amount of labeled data to just 1000 vice 10,000 labeled documents, achieved by labeling entire documents rather than individual fields.  This is done by first visually comparing two different documents, determining if they contain the same information, and then asking a single question about the format of the documents as a whole.  This results in a significant reduction in labeling costs, from $2.50 to $0.60 per example, for a dataset that is now also much less expensive to scale.  This is further demonstrated by applying this technique to a dataset of real-world documents, achieving similar performance to traditional labeling methods.  This could make it possible to label datasets that would otherwise be too expensive with the cost of high-quality features.  This research is also of interest from a theoretical perspective, formally defining the challenge of labeling datasets from a small number of visually rich documents, and showing that this can be efficiently solved with a novel document-format-learning algorithm. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. Furthermore, we explore various marking strategies and discover a straightforward method to promptly identify signals in real-time, without compromising classification performance. This achievement positions us well for the enhanced sensitivity of future gravitational wave detectors and their anticipated high detection rates. We anticipate our results to contribute positively to the emergence of multi-messenger astronomy. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unrecorded in Electronic Health Records, which are typically used as a marker for health disparities. A major constraint in addressing healthcare disparities is the lack of standardized and comprehensive data on social determinants of health. Due to the diverse nature and unstructured format of SDoH data, traditional approaches are often ineffective. We introduce an innovative marker-based framework that can quickly and effectively identify relevant information from unstructured texts within clinical notes. This framework is particularly well-suited for detecting markers associated with low prevalence conditions or certain comorbidities, which are common in certain patient populations and often indicative of a broader SDoH. We demonstrated the performance of this model on a range of clinically significant markers, including those related to the healthcare access and living situations of patients, and showed that it can learn to identify more complex social determinants of health, such as community mobility and health-related behaviors, by leveraging pre-trained language models and efficient neural network architectures. These developments have the potential to accelerate the development of practical and scalable methods for extracting comprehensive and marker-based data on social determinants of health from clinical notes. We hope this work will also serve as a starting point for researchers and healthcare organizations to build upon and contribute to existing knowledge in this field. We have made our implementations and results freely available for reference and use. Due to the diverse nature of SDoH data, the challenge of designing effective learning tasks and models cannot be overstated. In this work, we chose to focus on the marker-based approach, which involves identifying specific markers or aspects of SDoH within clinical notes. We recognized the significance of contextual information in clinical notes, which can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the identified markers, and the importance of validating the performance of deep learning models on a broader range of SDoH data. We selected seven prominent challenges in the NLP4MedSeq dataset, which include identifying risk factors, detecting the intensity of health issues, predicting safe medication doses, identifying necessary interventions, estimating the risk of complications, determining the effectiveness of treatments, and forecasting the likelihood of adherence; and recognized the value of pre-trained language models in the marker-based framework we developed. Furthermore, we extracted relevant information on the named entities, detected the aspect of health described in the clinical notes, and confirmed the ability of our model to process longer sequences of clinical notes.
