This study is centered on a key finding from a prior paper, where the optimal swimming speed of a scallop was determined by considering the squared differences between its contraction and extension cycle durations. To gain insight into these results, we was to model the scallop's dynamics during both cycle phases. For the purpose of this study, we developed a simplified model that could potentially be applied to various aquatic animal species that move in a eel-shaped manner. With this model, we examined two specific scenarios: one scenario in which the scallop maintains its position, and another scenario in which it moves optimally. Through both analytical and numerical methods, we derived and validated the formula for the optimal speed obtained from the model. Furthermore, we investigated how the scallop's body shape, contractile force, viscosity, and the resistance it encounters affect its optimal movement speed. The results from this study are consistent with previous research findings and provide a more in-depth analysis of the optimal movement strategy for the scallop model. The model also reveals the importance of the scallop's ability to adjust the speed at which it changes phase. This ability, which is linked to the phase transition rate, is shown to have a significant impact on the scallop's movement speed. The model is then applied to a scenario in which the scallop is subject to an external force, such as that produced by a fluctuating water current. The results from this study show that the scallop's optimal movement speed is affected by the amplitude of the current, but this effect varies depending on the frequency of the current and the scallop's own dynamics. The study also examines the precision of the optimal speed formula derived from the model and finds that this precision is significantly improved when the phase transition rate is high. The model is then used to investigate the optimal movement strategy for a scallop in which the contraction and extension cycle durations are significantly different. To better understand these findings, we developed an agent-based model to simulate individual behavior in an idealized city, establishing a framework that could be applied to other urban settings. Our study provides valuable insights for urban planners and policymakers, highlighting the importance of adapting to the evolving needs of urban residents in the face of unexpected events and their lasting impacts. The core-accretion model remains the most widely accepted theory for the formation of massive protostars. However, determining the duration of their growth phase presents a significant challenge. While early stages can be mapped using the submillimeter continuum, the inner regions during the main-accretion phase are in a different frequency range, accessible only through observations of molecular line spectra. A study of six massive protostars in the $H$-band shows that their spectra contain multiple high-velocity components, suggesting that massive protostars grow episodically. The merging of accretion streams, rather than gravitational collapse alone, can also explain the observed velocities. A statistical analysis of the detected velocities in the $H$-band, combined with previous findings from molecular line spectra, reveals a bimodal distribution. While some protostars have low velocity ranges, others have significantly higher velocities above 0.1 km/s, indicating that the growth of massive protostars can occur at a constant rate up to 10$^{-6}$ M$_{\odot}$/year for masses above 10 M$_{\odot}$. This research also discovers that the ratio of total to continuum accretion in the $H$-band is 10-100 times greater than found at submillimeter wavelengths, implying a significant increase in disk surface density during the main-accretion phase. The estimated timescales for the growth of the protostars range from 100 years for masses up to 8 M$_{\odot}$, and surprisingly, above 10 M$_{\odot}$. The research yields an intriguing correlation between the ratio of total to continuum accretion and the duration of the growth phase, suggesting that the most massive protostars in the sample have the lowest accretion rates and longest timescales. The findings of episodic accumulation and mergers during the growth of massive protostars have significant implications for the core-accretion model, and the discovery of multiple high-velocity components in the $H$-band can be used as a new indicator of the duration of the growth phase in the formation of these stars. We investigate a class of local operators, characterized by their wedge-local properties, and establish the principles of Haag-Kastler axiomatic quantum field theory. These operators can be derived from a family of endomorphisms on the algebra of observables, which are compatible and consistently consistent, and can be used to describe the behavior of particles in an expanding universe. Building on the work of Buchholz and Brunetti, we demonstrate that the representation of these endomorphisms is superselection sector-equivalent, and we develop a net of wedge-local observables through the application of these endomorphisms, while ensuring the satisfaction of the Haag-Pipka distortion principle. This construction enables the reconstruction of the net from its local properties, and we establish the existence of local, Poincaré-group-preserving wedge-local observables. We also show that the associated states generated by these observables satisfy the weak energy condition, and that they are of the Hadamard type, with their properties dependent on the Poincaré group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the net of wedge-local observables is of the Haag-Kastler type, and we investigate its connection to the principle of local covariance. This involves proving a theorem on the equivalence of wedge-local observables and scalar products of charged fields, and deriving consequences for the net of wedge-local observables from the properties of these fields. Building on these results, we discuss the implications for massive, higher-spin particles and their associated endomorphisms, and we outline the further investigations required. Additionally, we include an appendix on the application of Poincaré group generators to interacting local observables, and their derived Haag-Kastler nets. This involves explaining how the Poincaré group acts on the algebra of observables, and demonstrating the relevance of this action to the construction of local, Poincaré-group-preserving wedge-local observables. This, in turn, enables us to investigate the behavior of these observables over time, and to derive the associated states from the application of these observables at different times. This then allows us to discuss the connection between local, Poincaré-group-preserving wedge-local observables and local, time-like separated observables, and to outline the further investigations required in this area. We then establish the continuity of the differential shape realization map $\Psi$ from the space of differential shapes to the space of differential forms, and demonstrate that it forms a continuous module map. As a result, we derive the closure properties of differential shapes within the locally convex space setting. Furthermore, we derive and provide proof for the global Stokes formula on differential shapes. Additionally, we prove and outline the proof for the divergence theorem and the volume formula for differential shapes. Finally, we outline potential applications and extensions of these results in the context of differential shapes. Keywords: differential shapes, differential geometry, Stokes formula, divergence theorem, volume formula.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. Various techniques can be employed for this task, including deep learning methods, analyzing posting behavior, and detecting stylistic differences, but they are often hindered by difficulties in scaling and generalizing. We propose an innovative approach to detect false news on Reuters and Google News, leveraging the knowledge embedded within pre-trained language models, specifically BART and T5. By employing this knowledge for abstract generation through supervised learning, we enhance the discriminatory capacity of our models to identify false news. Experimental evaluations using two datasets yield positive results for our method, outperforming existing models and confirming the efficacy of using pre-trained language models for this task. Furthermore, our approach's versatility allows it to efficiently handle datasets of any scale, a critical advantage in the vast landscape of false news data. It is demonstrated that traditional notions of strong and uniform strong stationarity are equivalent when considering the impact of curvature. A more nuanced definition of relative stationarity is proposed in order to account for the effect of bending on spatially homogeneous Gaussian random fields. Conditions are then established to determine when a strongly relative stationary process can be identified as a traditional strong stationary process. A significant aspect of these conditions is the incorporation of the local integral operator of the generator of the Gaussian random field. The proposed definition of relative stationarity is a strengthening of the concept of local stationarity, and is investigated through the analysis of its relationship to local stationarity, as well as through the examination of its effects on spectral density and second-order characteristics. Additionally, the influence of the bending effect on the prediction theory of Gaussian random fields is explored. Linear prediction is shown to be an unbiased estimator of the true value, and is the best linear estimator under relative stationarity. The performance of linear prediction is compared to that under strong stationarity, and the difference is quantified in terms of the spectral density. Moreover, the impact of the bending effect on the estimation of stationary Gaussian random fields is investigated, and it is found that the traditional methods of spectral estimation remain valid under relative stationarity induced by bending. The research is illustrated through the analysis of a specific example of a strongly relative stationary Gaussian random field, following from the conditions established earlier, and the properties of its components are examined. A key aspect of these properties is that they reflect the effects of bending on the spatial behavior of the Gaussian random field, and its generators. The results provided are relevant to numerous applications that rely on spatially homogeneous and stationary Gaussian random fields, such as climate modeling, geostatistics, and remote sensing. To address these issues, researchers have proposed robust PCA (RPCA) models that aim to separate underlined sparse signals from noisy measurements.  Specifically, we have been investigating the well-posedness of the robust principal component analysis (RPCA) model that has been formulated as $\min_{\boldsymbol{x} \succeq 0, \boldsymbol{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n} \langle \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \rangle_1 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{y}\|_1$ under rotational ambiguities.  Our contribution is illustrated by solving a simplified rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-norm PCA that has already been applied to process images, resulting in an efficient and robust algorithm for sparse subspace recovery.  Notably, we have established the convergence rate of the proposed algorithm, $O(\frac{1}{\lambda^2} \log(\frac{\lambda \|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\|_1}{\tau}))^2$, where $\tau$ is the minimal eigenvalue of the covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.  Additionally, we have analyzed the proposed algorithm's behavior under noisy measurements, demonstrating that it produces a sparse subspace estimator with a convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\lambda^2} \log(\frac{\lambda \|\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{W}^T\boldsymbol{W}\|_1}{\tau}))^2$, where $\mathbf{W}$ is an orthonormal matrix representing the ambiguity of rotation.  Our findings are verified by various numerical experiments, including applications to image processing.  Interestingly, we have observed that the proposed algorithm yields comparable results with state-of-the-art methods, including OASIS and L1-LS, despite being much more straightforward to implement.  Our results demonstrate the proposed algorithm's linear convergence rate and its successful application to contaminated and outlier-present datasets, including images.  Notably, the proposed algorithm's simplicity and low computational cost make it an attractive solution for large-scale problems. Traditionally, semantic annotation is performed through human effort, but this can be expensive and time-consuming. Recent studies have investigated the potential of annotation tools assisted by pre-trained language models to reduce costs, improve efficiency, and accuracy. Our research focuses on the task of asking emotion-related questions using a dataset called NUSERQAs. To evaluate the performance of these assisted annotation methods, we conducted an online survey involving 60 participants who were presented with individually scored datasets. The results showed that methods assisted by BERT and other models yielded higher F1 scores compared to traditional methods, with BERT-based approaches also being more cost-effective and efficient. Notably, a BERT-supported interface achieved nearly identical results to those obtained through human annotations, with an F1 score of 0.645, which was only 0.008 lower than the score from human annotations. Overall, our research demonstrated the efficacy and cost-benefit advantages of using pre-trained language models for the annotation of emotion-related questions. Furthermore, a leading Chinese search engine company has already collaborated with our research team to adopt the BERT-supported annotation method for their search query classification task. Their feedback indicates that this approach has led to significant improvements in data quality, with cost savings of over $10,000 in the initial annotation stage alone. As a result of these positive outcomes, the company has expressed interest in expanding the scope of their search engine-related emotion-related question annotation task using the BERT-supported interface. Additionally, another Chinese company has shown interest in our research and has been granted a patent related to our BERT-supported annotation interface. On the other hand, some participants expressed concerns related to trust in the system, which we addressed through the implementation of a trust module. Furthermore, due to the limited scope of our initial experiment, we decided to conduct additional studies to validate the performance of the BERT-supported annotation interface with larger datasets, multiple emotion categories, and diverse annotation spans. Our supplementary findings confirmed the earlier results, with all BERT-based approaches delivering superior performance compared to traditional methods in all scenarios. Moreover, the results from the conducted surveys provided valuable insights into users' preferences, with over 70% of the participants expressing a willingness to pay up to $0.10 for each correctly annotated question using the BERT-supported interface. Our research has made significant contributions to the field of natural language understanding, particularly in the annotation of text, with the implementation of the trust module and the exploration of BERT-based annotation methods. The theory of contest equations has been a widely used framework for many years to model situations in which a beneficial resource must be allocated efficiently, such as in the dispersal of pollen or the spread of disease. The traditional approach assumes a linear or concave relationship between the contest and the resource in question, but fails to account for situations involving the spread of an infectious idea or the evolution of a population adapting to a changing environment, where an increase in one variable results in a proportional decrease in the other. This paper presents a new contest equation that generates an optimal outcome in a tournament over a totally ordered group of participants, where the ordering is based on the relative strength of each individual's contribution. We also provide a method for determining the equilibrium outcome in a general context, and apply this to several specific scenarios, including a Myerson-compatible model, a model from the work of Berg, Rota, and van de Rotten, as well as a model of the spread of an infectious idea. Furthermore, this paper is a follow-up to the authors' previous work on energy contests over groups of individuals with different levels of energy, where the contest is affected by the level of agreement among participants, and extends the previous results to a broader context, also known as the 'energized version'. The new contest equation is shown to be a special case of an 'energized' version, and the optimal outcome in a tournament over a totally ordered group of participants with different levels of energy is determined, providing a more comprehensive understanding of how different levels of energy influence the outcome in a contest. This research has implications for a wide range of applications, including the allocation of attention in social networks, the evolution of cooperation in prisoner's dilemma games, and the spread of ideas in innovation contests. Additionally, this paper contributes to the broader field of applied mathematics, particularly in the area of the biology of the Adams-Moser theorem, and provides a more detailed analysis of previous work on the contest equation, the Adams-Moser theorem, and its applications in biology and economics. We also provide an open-source MATLAB code for solving energy contest equations, as well as a new definition for optimality in a tournament over a totally ordered group of participants with different levels of energy, and demonstrate how the new definition can be applied to a wider range of contexts, including energy contests over groups of individuals with the same levels of energy, and a new model of the spread of an infectious idea, where the spread of the infection is affected by the level of energy of the infected individual. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. Further examination involving only the full duration datasets of both standard and asynchronous polars revealed a genuine, statistically significant difference in X-ray hardness ratios in favor of the asynchronous polars, not just trends. The findings suggest that there's a genuine difference in the X-ray emission patterns between standard and asynchronous polars' spectra. The detection rate bias in soft gamma-ray surveys might be attributed to the natural harder spectra of asynchronous polars rather than an artifact, as supported by this study's results. Furthermore, the greater whole-band counts of the asynchronous polars, observed in the full duration datasets, imply a connection between the primary X-ray emission component and the accretion streams in asynchronous polars. The greater extent of the accretion streams' overlap in asynchronous polars could be the physical reason for this greater whole-band counts, and consequently, the harder spectra. The greater whole-band counts of the asynchronous polars might also be linked to the greater hardness ratios in these systems, suggesting a connection between the primary X-ray emission component and the accretion streams' overlap rather than the impact of the secondary star's accretion streams. The difference in X-ray spectra between standard and asynchronous polars could also provide the basis for an objective method of identifying the former, as well as the latter, from their X-ray emission patterns. Furthermore, the greater whole-band counts of the asynchronous polars could be used as a sign of their asynchronous nature when coupled with other criteria. The possible association between harder spectra and the secondary star's mass, rather than the binary orbital period, is also discussed, as is the need for more in-depth studies into the physical properties of asynchronous polars. This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct approaches to solving Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems, namely a monolithic method and a segmented strategy. We discuss the fundamental principles of the RBM and both solution strategies, followed by an in-depth examination of two specific problem types: the monolithic solution of time-dependent problems and the segmented solution of steady-state problems. A significant focus lies on the reduction methods employed for both fluid and solid components. Furthermore, the project's objectives are illustrated through numerical experiments, covering both academic and industrial applications. The findings show the segmented RBM to be more suitable for complex FSI configurations, primarily due to its potential for greater flexibility in component interaction types. Nevertheless, the monolithic RBM remains the more conventional approach and is extensively validated in this project. The results for the industrial application were obtained with the support of an industrial partner and are subject to their approval for presentation at a conference. The project's scope also encompasses the development of an open-source Python toolbox for reduced-order modeling, titled PyFRB. This tool leverages the PyFR framework and expands on PyRB by integrating the monolithic and segmented reduction methods derived in this project. The source code of the Python toolbox has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. The project's scope extends to exploring new directions for the development of reduced-order models in the context of FSI, particularly regarding the segmented approach. One of the most promising approaches to detecting top quark production via elasticity involves analyzing events with a singular or dual highly energetic jet output. This occurs when the protons colliding at the Large Hadron Collider propel partons through a process of parton-parton interaction, resulting in a top quark pair with a significant momentum difference between them. As a consequence of the weak interaction, the two top quarks then decay into lighter particles that, due to their high energy, often consolidate into highly energetic jets. Identifying this phenomenon is exceptionally challenging because the signature closely mimics typical background processes that the production of top quarks frequently masks. Nonetheless, research indicates that machine learning algorithms can differentiate between these events with some degree of accuracy when trained on a comprehensive dataset. Consequently, a more in-depth analysis of data at the Large Hadron Collider may reveal evidence of top quark production via elasticity by combining traditional statistical methods with machine learning techniques. This would not only validate theoretical predictions made through the standard model and certain extensions but also provide insights into the fundamental properties of the top quark. Furthermore, researching this phenomenon also presents an opportunity to assess the LHC's capability to detect subtle signs of new physics processes that interact with top quarks in a manner that is different from standard model interactions. This in turn has important implications for future collider experiments that will be powered by more powerful and complex particle accelerators. This research paper outlines the strategy for detecting elastic top quark production at the Large Hadron Collider and explores the underlying theoretical principles that support this process. It is essential to note that the name 'elastic energy' refers to a specific process where the scattering angle between the two incoming partons is directly related to the scattering angle between the two outgoing particles produced as a result of the interaction in vacuum. This particular aspect of parton physics was initially described in a seminal paper published in 1979. This work also expands on earlier research and we are grateful to I. M. This research evaluates the performance of context-aware and adaptive wide-band deconvolution deep learning imaging (CADIDI) for the analysis of intra-cluster gas turbulence. Typically, deconvolution and deprojectation processes are assumed to be linear and precise, but even small measurement errors can significantly impact the resulting turbulence data. Given the complex nature of deconvolution and deprojectation, typical assumptions may lead to unrealistic turbulence findings. This study simulates such uncertainties using realistic configurations based on the Chandra observations of the Perseus cluster, a well-studied intra-cluster gas target. The aim is to identify any limitations or potential biases of the CADIDI method by comparing its outcomes with those from conventional approaches, as well as to determine the specific processes that affect turbulence analysis. The outcome shows that conventional deconvolution and deprojectation techniques can introduce artificial curves in the structure function data, while the CADIDI technique avoids this issue, with the document concluding that the primary challenge in accurately measuring intra-cluster gas turbulence lies with the process of deprojectation. The study also introduces a new quantity to evaluate the ambiguity of structure function measurement, with further research needed to fully understand the implications of measurement ambiguity on the use of power spectral density analysis. The study is the second in a series examining the CADIDI technique's performance. The first study found the method to be the most accurate among deep learning-based deconvolution techniques, although it was noted that more research is needed on this topic. The study is now being considered for publication in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society journal. An infinite graph $G$ contains a subgraph isomorphic to an infinite graph $H$ if there exists a subset $S$ of $G\'s vertices with a one-to-one correspondence to $H\'s vertices such that every edge between two vertices in $S$ corresponds to an edge between the corresponding vertices in $H$. A set $S$ with this property is called a Ramsey subset of $G$ for $H$. This paper focuses on determining the number of Ramsey subsets of a specific type of infinite graph, known as the infinite random graph $\om_\omega$. To do this, we first show that almost all non-directed trees have a number of Ramsey subsets equal to $2^{2^n}$ when $n$ is the number of distinct vertex levels. Then, we demonstrate that almost all non-directed trees with a specific structure also have a Ramsey subset number of $2^{2^n}$ when $n$ is the number of distinct vertex levels, although this result may not hold for directed trees with the same structure. Finally, the consistency of a larger Ramsey subset number is proven for certain infinite graphs, including non-directed trees with multiple distinct vertex levels by using forcing over models of set theory. Additionally, we examine properties of Ramsey upper richness, including its relation to other Ramsey properties and the structure of subgraphs defined by Ramsey upper richness. Lastly, this paper includes an open problem regarding the consistency of a larger Ramsey upper richness number for a specific type of infinite graph. Furthermore, we establish a new Ramsey upper richness number for a specific type of infinite graph, although its structure is quite complex, and even its edges are not necessarily symmetric. This resolution of the open problem was arrived at after demonstrating that certain subgraphs, including certain directed non-tree subgraphs, may have a Ramsey upper richness number equal to or greater than a certain exponential function of the number of distinct vertex levels. Additionally, we establish that almost all directed non-tree subgraphs have a Ramsey upper richness number no more than $2^{2^n}$ when $n$ is the number of distinct vertex levels. Finally, we conclude this paper by discussing its implications and several of its related open problems. This research was done with the support of National Science Foundation Grant No. DMS-2000240. This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called blink similarity, quantifying the similarity between blinking patterns, and successfully demonstrated its reliability through rigorous experiments requiring minimal labeled data. Notably, our eye-centered detection technique has demonstrated comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods employing entire facial images, while showcasing the feasibility of deploying AI-powered analytics in sensitive contexts. This research has far-reaching implications, as it paves the way for uncovering previously hidden information by analyzing blinking patterns, a long-overlooked aspect of human behavior. Furthermore, our work has inspired us to explore the eye-related potential of this idea, and we are excited to share our findings with the community. We warmly invite fellow researchers to collaborate with us and help us drive the eye-centered detection frontier forward.

Recent breakthroughs in the study of symmetric polynomials and integer parametrized systems have led to significant advancements in the analysis of finite groups represented by polynomials. By applying the theory of symmetric polynomials, the focus shifts from the original complex parameter space to a more manageable space of algebraic invariants. This transformation enables the use of sophisticated computational tools, specifically integer dynamic systems and computationally efficient decision trees, to determine vital properties of the groups. In this paper, we explore the concept of a "polynomial width" measure, which quantifies the complexity of defining a group using a finite set of polynomial equations based on the number of necessary monomials. We demonstrate that various finite groups can be represented with a low polynomial width and discuss the implications of this complexity measure for the underlying group structure. The interplay between polynomial width and other measures of computational complexity, such as the Betti numbers, is also examined, revealing connections and potential avenues for research in the field. The expertise gathered is further utilized to address an open problem posed by the study, centered on the query whether there exists a finite group that requires an exponentially large number of monomials to define it with a width of less than a specific, small number. The exploration of various candidates, including the cyclic groups, Abelian groups, and symmetric groups, is an essential part of the analysis, along with a discussion of the limitations imposed by the width constraint on the parameters of these groups. The examination of these classic groups is complemented by a review of more recent developments regarding the enumeration tasks for the general linear groups and the unitary groups, focusing on the implications of increased constraints on the size of the group, as seen in a broader statistical context. The exploration of these complex finite groups is supported by an extensive use of computational tools and expert knowledge, as reflected in the reference list containing over a hundred entries. The study of these groups is further enriched by an exploration of their non-trivial properties, including the dimension of the group, the number of non-trivial conjugacy classes, the number of non-trivial irreducible representations, and the several enumeration quantities that count various aspects of the group, such as the number of elements meeting specific criteria or the number of conjugacy classes containing elements with particular properties. The analysis of these properties is a key part of the research, with some of the quantities shown to scale polynomially with the group size, while others may scale exponentially or are shown to be bounded by a constant independent of the group size. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature detector, comprising a temperature-sensing unit and a digital processing module. The temperature-sensing unit features a novel sub-threshold PMOS-only circuit that provides an digital output following each power cycle, whereas the digital processing module employs two complementary counters to calculate the temperature based on the sensing unit's digital output. A 0.24°C resolution and $\pm$1.4°C inaccuracy are achieved with a 16-bit design, utilizing a single 1.8V supply voltage and operating in the 0.6V $\leq$ $V_{DD}$ $\leq$ 1.5V range. Furthermore, the design offers a compact footprint with a 42x26$\mu$m active area, low power consumption, and the ability to function in high-temperature applications due to its wide $V_{DD}$ operating range. This design serves as an appropriate temperature detection solution for memory and data storage systems. A 6um-wide N-channel transistor improves the design's stability in high-temperature applications, and its inclusion does not impact the performance or require additional area. The proposed temperature detector achieves a 0.24°C resolution, $\pm$1.4°C inaccuracy, and a 1.06nJ conversion energy per cycle, outperforming prior art. This design's efficacy is demonstrated through the fabrication of a test chip using a 180nm CMOS process. Experimental results from the test chip, evaluated at 1.2V $V_{DD}$ and 25°C, yield a 0.18°C typical error and a maximum error of 1.38°C, converging to the theoretical value within 1.3 cycles and featuring a 0.24°C $\pm$1.5°C inaccuracy before failing. This failure is attributed to a non-ideal cross-coupled CMOS latch in the 42x26$\mu$m temperature-sensing unit, whose improvement is also discussed. Furthermore, this design's suitability for mass storage systems is further validated through the successful operation of the temperature detector in a real-world application, a 1TB hard disk drive. The designed temperature detector is utilized as the detection mechanism for the "recalibrate" command, a critical function that ensures accurate temperature measurement. The execution of this command results in the convergence of a million 32-bit binary counters within 1.3 cycles, following which the temperature is calculated and displayed as 25.6°C. This field's behavior is often described using a set of linearized equations that ignore non-linear interactions. However, non-linear effects can become significant under certain conditions, such as in stars with strong magnetic fields. This paper examines the validity of the linearized framework by directly solving the full set of non-linear induction equations for ideal magnetic fluids. It demonstrates that the non-linear regime agrees with the linearized approach in a specific context - the stabilization of axisymmetric magnetic configurations. However, this agreement holds only when the Alfv\'en speed is constant across the star, a condition not typically met in stars undergoing significant polynomial expansion. The study implies that in such cases, the linearized framework may not accurately capture the long-term evolution of the star's magnetic field. This insight is relevant to low-mass stars like white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. It is also noteworthy that in stars where the Alfv\'en speed increases with distance from the center, the non-linear effects can actually destabilize axisymmetric magnetic configurations. This outcome might be linked to magnetic winds in young, rapidly rotating stars. The research extends the established criterion for stable magnetic forces in stars to cover the non-linear regime and provides a more precise definition of the stability requirement. Music education is a valuable tool for cultivating children's creativity, emotional intelligence, and cognitive abilities through song. Nonetheless, many young people are no longer exposed to music education due to funding cuts in community programs. COVID-19 pandemic-related restrictions also forced the closure of music venues, further compromising access to music education. In response to these challenges, we've developed Pied Piper, a VR experience for the Quest headset that introduces elementary school children to the basics of music composition using the Magical Piano, a innovative interface we've created. Through a series of engaging lessons and medleys, Pied Piper teaches fundamental music theory and encourages children to explore their imagination. To ensure the effectiveness of this educational program, we've conducted a thorough evaluation with over 220 participants, gathering valuable feedback from both casual and frequent users. Our results show that Pied Piper achieves its objectives by making music accessible to a wider audience and fostering a sense of pride and accomplishment in users. Furthermore, our analysis of the game's audio and video content reveals the presence of several cultural traditions, demonstrating the program's potential to promote musical diversity and inclusivity. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of traditional Godel logics, which in turn are based on the finitary Godel algebras. We examine various algebraic and relational structures that can represent Godel modal logics, considering their own structures as well as the underlying Godel algebras. Specifically, we investigate the equivalence of modal Godel logics defined by normal modal operators acting on countable structures, the applicability of the Canoniacal Invariant method, and the resulting canonical formulas. We also explore the connection between these canonical formulas and the first-order properties of the structures, as well as the degrees of complexity of the modal Godel logics determined by these canonical formulas. Additionally, we look at the application of the Sahlqvist connection to these modal Godel logics, including the process of finding canonical bases and axioms, and the identification of the primitive modal operators. We further discuss the preservation of the canonical formulas under the operation of taking canonical bases, and the relationship between these canonical formulas and the first-order properties of the structures. We also consider some of the limitations of these techniques, such as the issue of infinite complexity. We then move on to considering some of these issues in the context of simpler structures, such as the natural numbers, and the impact of changing the order of the Godel algebras, as well as the addition of new constants, on the modal logics and their canonical formulas. We also explore the application of these techniques to more complex structures, such as trees and the order theory of the integers, and the use of these methods to prove the completeness of these modal logics, as well as their decidability. We conclude by considering some of the open questions in this area, such as the issue of finite complexity, and the possibility of using these methods for more complex extensions of the basic Godel modal logic. We also discuss the background and the relevant previous work in this area, and the potential applications of these results, such as the potential for these methods to be used in other areas, such as the study of the complexity of the satisfiability problem, and the potential for these techniques to be used with other types of algebras, such as the extension of these methods to the intensional Godel algebras. The source of cosmic rays with energies exceeding 10^20 eV remains one of the most profound mysteries in astrophysics. A connection between high-energy cosmic rays and neutrino observations has been observed, with sources often associated with both phenomena. However, identifying the exact origins of these particles is a significant challenge. In this paper, we undertake a comprehensive analysis of extensive air showers caused by cosmic rays above 40 EeV, in an effort to discover potential links to neutrino detections as recorded by the ANTARES and IceCube neutrino detectors. Our statistical approach, utilizing a joint probability distribution to account for the positioning of neutrino sources, reveals that there are 19 reported extensive air showers that are within 10 degrees of known neutrino sources, a figure that exceeds the expected result by 4.5 standard deviations. Our study indicates that there is a statistically significant spatial association between neutrino sources and cosmic rays with energies above 40 EeV, at a level of 4.5σ. Furthermore, we found that 13 out of 14 detected neutrino sources have associated cosmic rays within 5 degrees, a phenomenon that is 4.7σ more likely to occur. Our research implies that a substantial fraction of cosmic rays with energies above 40 EeV originate from extragalactic sources. Moreover, we found that there is a spatial correlation between cosmic rays and neutrinos at a level of 7.5σ, a finding that is consistent with a vast, neutrino-dominated field scenario. Our study also reveals that there is a strong correlation between cosmic rays and neutrinos within such fields, at a level of 5.7σ. Additionally, we found that there is a significant discrepancy between the observed and expected cosmic ray densities near neutrino sources, at a level of 4.5σ, indicating that these sources are likely to be point-like or have a characteristic size of no more than 20 million light-years. Our study provides a framework for further research and offers insights into potential connections between high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos. It paves the way for more in-depth analyses that can provide a more comprehensive understanding of these enigmatic phenomena. Our analysis is primarily based on data collected by the Pierre Auger Observatory, with additional information from the ANTARES and IceCube neutrino detectors. This phenomenon is unlike the usual Rayleigh-Benard case where the same density liquids create rings of vapor. Research indicates that the most unstable mode of the system is at an angle of $\pi/6$ with the vertical when the curvature is not a factor and at an angle of $\pi/2$ with the vertical when the curvature is a strong factor. This relationship leads to the conclusion that the influence of the curvature on the most unstable wavenumber in the Curved Rayleigh-Benard problem will become stronger as the curvature increases. In neural machine translation, the focus of the model on generating each word can be controlled by an attention mechanism that maps the entire input sequence to a series of attention vectors. However, current attention mechanisms treat every word equally, which can lead to suboptimal results due to the sequential nature of translation. A more effective attention mechanism is therefore proposed, where a set of focus attention mechanisms, working in sequence on the input sentence, can model the sequential relationship between words. The proposed Focal-Attention network achieves state-of-the-art performance on WMT14 English-to-German and WMT14 English-to-French translation tasks. Moreover, it is also demonstrated that the Focal-Attention network's ability to model sequential relationships can be useful in modeling the sequential nature of target sentences, particularly in situations with long target sentences. The results show little difference in efficiency and model complexity when compared to standard attention-based neural machine translation. The model's ability to capture sequential relationships is verified through various attention visualisation techniques. The proposed Focal-Attention framework can be applied to other sequence-generation tasks such as text classification, which is shown through additional experiments. The source code of the proposed model has been made publicly available online. The Focal-Attention network offers a more realistic representation of the generation process than the standard neural machine translation method, which could provide valuable insights into the underlying processes of language generation. The proposed model may also offer an explanation for various linguistic phenomena such as the difficulty of translating long sentences and the need for sentence planning in second language learners. The Focal-Attention network can be seen as an empirical verification of the theory of sentence structure proposed by Chomsky, which posits that the structure of a sentence is determined by the order of the focus of each word. The Focal-Attention network also raises new research questions concerning the application of linguistic theories to machine learning models and the use of attention mechanisms as a diagnostic tool for underlying linguistic processes. The proposed Focal-Attention network can be used to diagnose the focus structure of test data, which can be used to predict the performance of the model on unseen data. The model's ability to model the focus structure of sentences can also be used to increase the diversity of generated sentences, which is achieved through the proposed Diversity-Focal-Attention network. The Diversity-Focal-Attention network generates sentences with a higher average diversity in terms of both syntax and semantics when compared to standard attention-based neural machine translation. The significant disparity between computing and networking advancements led to a need for a higher-level abstraction, prompting the development of grid computing. Researchers attempted to bridge this gap through the concept of a computational grid, relying on the metaphor of a power grid. They drew inspiration from the translation of electrical signals into a common language, allowing seamless energy distribution. This paper follows the evolution of grid computing, focusing on the development of the next generation of computational infrastructures. It emphasizes the value of viewing computing systems through the lens of translation, an idea first proposed in the late 1990s. This philosophical perspective has driven the design of modern distributed systems, such as clouds and edge computing frameworks, and has contributed to the advancement of programming models and applications. This perspective has also given rise to the concept of edge-as-a-grid, which the authors introduce in this paper. They present a case study on moving application workloads to the edge, utilizing the translation framework to design an adaptive, distributed system. This approach is then compared with other methodologies, revealing the benefits of the translation framework in the development of distributed systems. Finally, the author contemplates the future implications of this perspective on the design of computational infrastructures. This paper will be of interest to the broader scientific community as an historical analysis of the evolution of computational infrastructures. It also provides a reference for researchers and practitioners who are familiar with the development of grid computing but less familiar with its underpinning transformational approach. A new cosmological model that integrates two types of dark matter-energy has been proposed by the authors. This model, which involves a constant dark energy component and a dissipative unified dark substance with both viscous and relativistic properties, is capable of explaining the current observed dynamics of the Hubble constant and the cosmic quenching phenomenon. By contrast to the $\Lambda$CDM model, their new model achieves this explanation without the need to interpret the'matter density parameter' $Ω_m$ in an non-intuitive manner. Rather, $Ω_m$ in this model directly represents the ratio of matter to total unified substance density. A numerical solution for the Hubble parameter in this model has been derived by the authors and it fits well with data from supernovae, the cosmic microwave background, and Hubble diagram plots. Furthermore, a numerical analysis indicates that this model can be distinguished from the $\Lambda$CDM model through future cosmic microwave background experiments with enhanced resolution. Additionally, this model's predictions for the power spectrum of matter density fluctuations are consistent with those of the $\Lambda$CDM model as evidenced by the authors' Fisher matrix calculations. A solution to the equations of this model has been derived by an exact numerical method developed by Benson and Kamionkowski, and a related perturbation theory. This has implications that the model's fluctuations in matter density could be described by a Gaussian distribution, in accordance with the $\Lambda$CDM model. This paper presents an extension of a previous model proposed by Boehmer and Hurn, and it has been submitted to Physical Review D for peer review and consideration. The model it presents has several novel features, including an equation for the evolution of matter density fluctuations derived from its underlying theory, and a theoretical prediction for the amplitude of these fluctuations. This model also predicts a phase of slow cosmological evolution, similar to that in the $\Lambda$CDM model, and it has been tested against a wide range of observational data from supernovae, the cosmic microwave background, and Hubble diagram plots. The model's new equation for the evolution of matter density fluctuations has been analyzed using the authors' own numerical method, and it has been shown that this equation is consistent with the standard theory of perturbation theory. It has also been demonstrated that the model can be distinguished from the $\Lambda$CDM model through future cosmic microwave background experiments with enhanced resolution. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a desire for personal growth.  Unfortunately, many children lose their innate curiosity during their school years due in part to ineffective teaching methods, standardization, and learning environments that fail to inspire wonder and a love of learning.  This paper introduces an intriguing theoretical concept, "Curiosity Depth," that offers a nuanced perspective on the complex and multifaceted nature of curiosity.  This novel perspective is comprised of three interconnecting layers, drawn from the works of Hidi (2001) and Ainley (2007), and is designed to provide a comprehensive framework for examining the intricate inner workings of curiosity.  To validate this framework, the researchers developed and implemented a scoring system for quantifying Curiosity Depth.  This study employed this scoring system to investigate how three-dimensional geometry learning experiences influenced curiosity in a population of 61 eighth-grade students. Gaussian models representing functions based on Mat\'ern kernels have been widely used in various settings, including spatial and temporal applications.  While Mat\'ern kernels provide a comprehensive framework, their limitations arise when trying to model non-stationarity.  Recent developments in graph theory and statistical modeling have sparked interest in expanding Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to complex graph domains.  This work contributes novel constructions of non-stationary Mat\'ern Gaussian processes for exploring relationships within complex datasets, particularly-suited for exploratory data analysis.  Our non-stationary extensions of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes are shown to be statistically consistent when estimating parameters, and our new kernels also facilitate efficient and effective prediction.  To illustrate the practical advantages of these constructions, our research includes an analysis of synthetic data and a real-world application involving network analysis.  Our findings demonstrate that our non-stationary Mat\'ern Gaussian processes exhibit better performance compared to traditional approaches, leading to potential applications across multiple domains.  Our work on non-stationary Mat\'ern Gaussian processes is now publicly available through the RodyKit Python library Ryoko, making it easily accessible for further development and extension by the research community.  In addition, we outline several potential research extensions and pathways for future exploration within this exciting research area.  Our work is a product of the Kyoto University Statistics Initiative, a multidisciplinary research program dedicated to developing statistical theories, methods, and models, and we gratefully acknowledge the support received from this initiative. This problem has significant implications as it impacts the neutrino and dark matter direct detection experiments, as well as the status of the weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) paradigm. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it is labor-intensive and requires highly skilled professionals. Computer-based automatic nucleus detection can aid in the efficient analysis of histopathology images, but the challenging nature of this task has hindered significant progress. To overcome this obstacle, we present an automated nucleus identification system called W-Net, which leverages a novel combination of techniques to achieve exceptional performance. W-Net integrates SegNet's dense connectivity pattern and ResNet's nonlinear feature learning, while its second stage uses a detailed feature map to refine and validate identified nuclei. We evaluated W-Net using 20 test images, obtaining a remarkable 94.1% accuracy rate for nucleus detection, which we verified through comprehensive experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings suggest that W-Net delivers superior performance, outperforming existing approaches by a significant margin. Furthermore, we found that removing the refinement module in W-Net results in a reduction in accuracy by as much as 9.3%, underscoring the importance of this feature in achieving optimal results. To facilitate replication and advancement of nucleus detection techniques, we publicly released our dataset and W-Net implementation. To further improve the accuracy of W-Net, we suggest exploring alternative nonlinear layers and incorporating autoregressive models for enhanced nucleus segmentation. Despite its exceptional performance, W-Net's efficiency can be improved through the use of less computationally intensive convolutional network architectures. We look forward to contributions from the research community that address these potential optimizations. In addition to superior detection accuracy, W-Net offers real-world applicability, which we demonstrated through the integration of W-Net into a comprehensive colon cancer diagnosis system called CDS. Through CDS, we successfully diagnosed colon cancer using histopathology images, which we presented at the IEEE ISBI 2017 Challenge, where our solution ranked first among five participating teams. We openly share our CDS implementation, which we believe will benefit the research community and contribute to the advancement of cancer diagnosis technology. Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. This knowledge can be used to make data-driven predictions about the effects of anti-inflammatory treatments on host-tissue dynamics. This research highlights the value of combining theoretical modeling with experimental and clinical knowledge for a comprehensive understanding of COVID-19's multi-scale host-dynamics. However, the reliability of these programs is consistently compromised due to their complex and ever-changing nature. To address this concern, this paper introduces HELMHOLTZ, a validation tool tailored for Tezos smart contracts leveraging refinement types. Our approach is distinct from other approaches, such as static validation, dynamic testing, and formal verification, offering a more practical solution. By utilizing a type of refinement types called set refinement types, which are supported in the Tezos smart contract language, Compile and Reflect, we can express invariants about the program's input and output data types. Notably, GCNNs have demonstrated superior accuracy in detecting gravitational wave signals, which are essentially events represented as non-standard graph structures. This success of GCNNs can be attributed to their innate ability to adapt to data structures and effectively mitigate the aliasing phenomenon inherent in gravitational wave signals. This paper delves into the underlying reasoning behind the efficacy of GCNNs on gravitational wave data and explains how the network's convolutional structure serves as a form of matched filtering. Furthermore, this paper explores the possibility of replacing GCNNs with alternative structures, such as Self-Convolutive Neural Networks (SCNNs) or Graph Attention Networks (GATs), and evaluates their performance. The results indicate that SCNNs and GATs also yield optimal results, which provides a more comprehensive understanding of GCNNs' success. A primary application lies in CT reconstruction from ultra-low-dose CT scans, a challenging task that involves prioritizing noise reduction and detail preservation. Deep learning-based solutions can be delivered through an unsupervised learning approach using CycleGAN, which enables the direct generation of high-dose CT images from low-dose CT scans. However, existing methods suffer from limitations such as the requirement for paired training data, the inability to handle over-smoothing, and the generation of non-realistic images. To address these issues, we present a novel AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN framework, which leverages AdaIN layers for both feature extraction and synthesis. By integrating two novel modules – the Feature Refining Module and the Synthesis Refining Module – we enhance both the encoder and decoder of the generator. Specifically, the Feature Refining Module is positioned before the discriminator's encoder to compress features efficiently, while the Synthesis Refining Module is placed within the decoder to refine the feature reconstruction. By employing a discriminator and adopting an AdaIN-switchable strategy, we swap the AdaIN layers' freeze and learn states during training, resulting in a more effective learning of unsupervised constraints. Comprehensive comparisons with the current state-of-the-art methods have validated the superior performance of our proposed framework in terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics. Furthermore, our method's efficiency has been demonstrated through a practical application of ultra-low-dose CT reconstruction from paired scanning protocols. In multi-task reinforcement learning, learning to solve one task can facilitate solving another. However, a significant challenge arises when multiple tasks share similar goal states - a problem known as catastrophic interference. This issue exists in real-world scenarios, such as robotics, where goal states often overlap. To address this problem, we propose a solution called the Modular Network for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning. This solution involves dividing the world into independent goal networks for each task and using a shared policy network to determine which network to use. By utilizing goal networks specific to each task, our solution prevents destructive interference and facilitates efficient learning. Our approach outperforms existing methods in a variety of multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios, including both simple and complex worlds with various numbers of tasks and sensory inputs. These include a complex 3D multi-task maze and a complex robotic mountain car problem. Our approach also compares favorably to non-modular models, such as separate policy networks and shared policy and value networks, in both sample efficiency and task performance. These benefits come with minimal additional memory requirements, making our solution an attractive choice for a wide range of multi-task reinforcement learning applications. These include learning in multiple robotic arms, learning in the presence of multiple competing agents, and solving a complex mountain car problem with multiple lanes. These results provide a strong foundation for future research into the advantages of modular solutions in multi-task reinforcement learning. These solutions have the potential to address a broader range of challenges in this field, such as the problem of discovering separate goal networks, the issue of goal networks that are too specific or too general, and the challenge of adapting model-based multi-task reinforcement learning to dynamic and changing worlds. These issues are investigated in an accompanying technical report available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04299. The problem of selecting samples in sequence from a large dataset located in a high-dimensional space is a persistent challenge, especially when resources are limited and the data's quality varies significantly across different subspaces. This research introduces an innovative technique called Spatially Equitable Sampling (SESAM) to tackle this issue head-on. SESAM employs a unique combination of random walk and importance sampling to identify samples that are not only dispersed uniformly within the data set but also situated in a way that facilitates efficient learning from the data. We demonstrate through theoretical and practical experiments that SESAM's equity-based approach results in the selection of high-quality training batches, even in complex real-world scenarios. Furthermore, SESAM is an adaptable and user-friendly method that offers an equitable training solution for neural networks without requiring any significant modifications to existing code. The code for the sesam package used in these experiments and more is now available on the GitHub platform. Additionally, a paper outlining the details of SESAM's experiments and more has been made publicly available on the arXiv preprint server. We have also included an additional appendix in the updated code and paper. We hope this research inspires the development of novel techniques for identifying equitable samples in sequence from diverse datasets. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in various applications including compressed sensing, deblurring, super-resolution, and radiology using tomography. Because the process often involves finding a minimum among possible solutions, conventional algorithms can be computationally expensive for large-scale complex images. We propose a novel framework that finds an optimal solution within a feasible set by formulating the problem as finding a probability measure representing the restored image. This framework is particularly effective for real-time image restoration but may not guarantee theoretical minimality. To address this limitation and improve the algorithm's performance, we introduce an iterative learning algorithm that reduces the noise effect and overcomes some underlying constraints. The algorithm's benefits include faster convergence, removal of artificial biases, and increased robustness to noise and model deviations. We apply our algorithm to various numerical examples and realistic experiments, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods. The code is openly accessible on the Learning Factors Networks website. The paper also provides a detailed analysis, including a discussion on possible extensions to multichannel image restoration. Traditionally, massive MIMO systems use a direct transmission method for beam training, yet this approach can be impractical due to the long distance between the anchor node and the target and the high directional requirements for THz waves. An alternative is to utilize a multi-hop approach with lower frequency waves for intermediate transmissions. However, this can lead to suboptimal performance if the chosen beams aren't ideal, resulting in reduced throughput and extended transmission times. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed that leverages reinforcement learning to select the best beams at each intermediate node, maximizing the overall transfer rate and outperforming existing methods. Simulations show that this approach can achieve up to 75% better results than traditional techniques and is particularly beneficial in scenarios with a large number of possible beams. The proposed system also demonstrates its applicability in dynamic scenarios through the implementation of a learning algorithm that adapts to changes in the environment, such as node movements, reducing transmission costs and further improving efficiency. The developed system architecture is called Multi-Hop Reinforcement Learning Transmission (MH-RTT). The results obtained from MH-RTT are comparable to those from a holistic optimization approach but with the advantage of being more flexible and easier to implement. WN's success in the raw waveform generation task can be attributed to its capability to model both long-term and short-term dependencies. In our experiments, a Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolution Neural Network (PECNN) was implemented as a QPNet front-end, and our results indicate that this design achieves comparable performance to the standard WaveNet while significantly enhancing model interpretability and the ability to control pitch-dependent outputs. Furthermore, our study illuminates the limitations and potential of the deep autoregressive and wavefunction-based generative models, respectively, in modeling the inherent quasi-periodic properties of audio signals. We introduce a refined version of the $\mu$-calculus with the addition of a limited and well-defined set of variables, which can either be part of a scalar or a vectorial structure. The added complexity allows for the expression of numerous NP-complete problems that cannot be addressed with the standard $\mu$-calculus. The added variables can be seen as introducing references to specific points within a given counterpath, essentially equipping the $\mu$-calculus with a form of backlinks. In the context of set theory, we demonstrate that the resulting mu-calculus with variables, which we term $\mu_{\text{ent}}$, has an interpretability equivalent to the complexity class PSPACE, in contrast to the standard $\mu$-calculus which has a lower complexity of NP. We also provide a comparison with other extensions of the $\mu$-calculus, such as the $\mu$-calculus with counting, and show that $\mu_{\text{ent}}$ can address all PSPACE problems that can be solved with the $\mu$-calculus with counting, but there are problems that can be solved with the $\mu$-calculus with variables but not with the $\mu$-calculus with counting. Furthermore, we establish that the addition of variables to the modal $\mu$-calculus with benefits also extends to the Cooper's Presburger Arithmetic along Counterpaths ($\text{CAP}$), which is a more comprehensive theory that encompasses the properties of counterpaths, including the diagnosis of counterpaths. The added variables to $\text{CAP}$, which we term $\text{CAP}_{\text{ent}}$, allow for the resolution of numerous NP-complete problems but with the trade-off of only being able to determine the existence of a path with a specific property, rather than the full specification of that path. Lastly, we provide an implementation of $\mu_{\text{ent}}$ and $\text{CAP}_{\text{ent}}$ in the form of a Prolog-based framework, which we make available for download. This implementation can serve as a reference for the execution of mu-calculus with variables, which we term mu-ent, and its extension to the field of counterpaths, which we term cap-ent. This reference implementation can be accessed at: https://github.com/robardj/mu-calculus-ent/tree/v1.1.0.3. Additionally, we include an updated version of the benchmark suite developed by Halpern

Characterizing colorectal polyps histology is crucial to determine their potential for cancer development. Current computational approaches rely heavily on features extracted from convolutional neural networks, yet a significant obstacle is the scarcity of high-quality, annotated colorectal polyps datasets. To address this issue, our UniToPatho dataset has been created in collaboration with multiple Italian universities and medical centers, involving expert pathologists who annotated and graded 8476 regions within 104 whole-slide images according to the Hamburger classification system. This dataset distinguishes itself from others like the Figlio et al. dataset which only provides binary annotations for malignancy, making UniToPatho the most comprehensive colorectal polyps dataset available to date. UniToPatho demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of a strategy that combines low-resolution pre-training and subsequent local expert annotation, allowing for the utilization of economical lightweight models in image annotation tasks. Our findings show that a combination of a ResNet50 pre-trained on the entire dataset, followed by expert annotation of local areas, yields 73.1% overall accuracy and outperforms alternative strategies. Furthermore, UniToPatho enables evaluation of computational methods for colorectal polyps grading, a process that is normally carried out by experienced pathologists but is currently not standardized, resulting in varying accuracy across different studies. To facilitate comparison with existing studies, we employed two main approaches to grade polyps based on the annotations provided, resulting in overall accuracies of 65.4% and 68.5%, respectively. To facilitate access to these annotations, we developed a web-based platform that enables users to explore our results and the underlying annotations. UniToPatho not only fills a significant gap in the field of colorectal polyps research but also serves as a prime example of a collaborative project involving multiple Italian universities and medical centers. The expertise of these pathologists, combined with their access to whole-slide images, was instrumental in producing these high-quality annotations. As such, we believe that this project has the potential to drive further advancements in computational pathology research. The annotations created as part of this project have been made available under a permissive license to accommodate the needs of all contributors and the broader research community. To ensure the reliability of these annotations, a rigorous review process involving multiple independent experts was conducted, as is normal practice in computational pathology challenges. In accordance with established best practices, we employed a train-test-split approach to divide the annotations into training and testing sets, ensuring that the identities of the polyps used for training and testing remained unknown to all pathologists

A novel numerical strategy has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. To solve the time-domain problem, an explicit and an implicit expansion in time are alternately employed for successive short-time periods, with corresponding burden on computational memory. To enhance efficiency further, the method is implemented using an adaptive finite element approach, featuring variable time step sizes and adaptive mesh refinement based on local frequency information. A series of computational experiments validate the method's performance and accuracy. Notably, the method excels when dealing with large-sized problems and complex geometries, such as scattering in the presence of multiple radiating sources, three-dimensional inhomogeneous layers, and stochastic alligator-shaped interfaces. The developed code is an open-source finite element solver for time-domain scattering problems, with potential applications in seismic imaging, seismic resonance, and seismology. The code's performance is comparable to or outperforms existing state-of-the-art solvers in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The introduced approach may also be applicable to other hyperbolic partial differential equations, such as the seismic imaging problem. The code's source is available at https://github.com/CFE-Research-Group/CFE-FEM-3D. Our analysis of oxygen isotope ratios from pyroxene grains within the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites offers new insights into the accretion process of planetesimals in the inner solar system. By comparing these values to those of CV chondrites, we have made some notable observations. Firstly, the majority of pyroxene grains from the Chelyabinsk airbrush have isotopically similar oxygen compositions, ranging from -0.26 to +0.36 delta SIMS value (+0.16 on average), which is consistent with the narrow distributions seen in individual petrographic types of CV chondrites (up to 0.5 delta SIMS value). Secondly, a more extensive range of values was found for pyroxene grains from the Benenitra strewn field (-0.87 to +1.05 delta SIMS value, +0.24 on average). Although some experts might attribute these results to partial equilibration, our research instead suggests that the narrow range of isotope ratios in the Chelyabinsk airbrush and broader range in Benenitra could be indicative of planetesimals that experienced inner solar system formation processes. In the case of Benenitra, the broader distribution might be attributed to the longer accretion period of its parent body, supported by higher petrographic texture variability and larger chondrule sizes when compared to the Chelyabinsk population. Our findings provide new evidence for the concept of "damp accretion" proposed by Cieslak et al. (2007) and have significant implications for the formation and early evolution of planetesimals in the inner solar system. Furthermore, our research suggests that the "damp accretion" model can also explain the observed variations in the sizes of planetesimals, such as the larger sizes of asteroid 16 Psyche, which could be the remnant core of a planetesimal that formed through "damp accretion". This research provides new insights into the inner solar system's early formation and development, and its unique "damp accretion" process may have significant implications for the formation of planetary cores worldwide. This "damp accretion" process could have contributed to the formation of numerous iron-rich planetary cores in the inner solar system by allowing the sticking of like-isotopic grains, leading to large solid bodies forming through the accumulation of numerous small building blocks. This allows the model to generate high-quality audio translations in any target language. Our model achieves remarkable translation accuracy with just text-based training and delivers superior results to traditional pivot-based translation methods. Notably, our proposed approach also results in significantly more natural-sounding audio translations. Our model's ability to model both language and speech proves highly beneficial for topics that are not explicitly covered during training, where other approaches quickly decline in performance. Our method is particularly useful for topics that are difficult to define or describe, where other approaches struggle with accuracy. A cutting-edge convolutional neural network called ChestX-ray14 has made significant progress in identifying various conditions from chest X-rays, but its limitations become apparent when it attempts to diagnose complex respiratory diseases whose presence often indicates a broader range of abnormalities.  Rather than diagnosing specific conditions from these images, we propose an alternative approach – one that uses a generative adversarial network to create realistic chest X-rays tailored to specific diagnosis results from the ChestX-ray14 dataset.  We demonstrate through self-supervised training on generated images, we can successfully train a classifier from scratch.  Notably, our model's performance surpasses traditional transfer learning on several benchmarks.  We also explore the capabilities of our model by using it to create images from various conditions and then having a classifier trained on these new images.  The code for our model is available at https://github.com/ghm-2019/illness-aware-editing.  We hope this work will contribute to creating realistic respiratory disease cases for future research and lay the foundation for advancing medical imaging knowledge via iterative editing and generation tasks.  We anticipate future studies will investigate more sophisticated imaging transformations and the development of novel imaging-based expertise through expert interactions with edited images.  We hope future researchers will build upon our work by exploring various editing techniques and the potential connections between medical experts' insights and the features of generated images.  We also hope to collaborate with leading chest X-ray specialists to gain a deeper understanding of the visual characteristics associated with specific respiratory conditions as identified in the ChestX-ray14 dataset.  We anticipate such expertise will be essential in addressing potential limitations in the current dataset, such as the lack of annotations for specific lung pathologies, which, if addressed, could, in turn, contribute to creating more realistic and detailed chest X-rays.  We also hope to explore the broader implications of our work in the context of advancing medical imaging knowledge via iterative editing and generation tasks. We introduce FastEvaluatingDirectMethod (FEDM) for a wide range of Newtonian potentials in two dimensions, enabling rapid evaluation of potentials and their gradients at a desired point within a given planar domain defined by $n$ order-$k$ Bezier curves. Our main innovation is in efficiently describing the boundary of the domain, and subsequent progress in computing the shadow and its development. We apply these insights to develop an exact yet efficient algorithm for determining the minimum distance from a point to the boundary, as well as the amount of the domain visible from the point. We also present a novel algorithm for the Feasible Directions method, a classic nonlinear optimization algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of FEDM through several concrete examples and make the implementation publicly available along with an accompanying user guide. We additionally discuss how to adapt FastEvaluatingDirectMethod to meet the requirements of two specific use cases: one for domains defined by higher-order Bezier surfaces, and another for domains defined by convex polygons. The implementation is also compatible with the Gadget-3 multi-physics platform. We include an analysis of the algorithm's computational costs and provide an update on a previous related study. Finally, we explore potential extensions to FastEvaluatingDirectMethod for a broader range of applications.
